[p-3882]

**Surat al-Isra'**

It is also called Surat Bani Isra'il and Surat Subhan. There is no reported disagreement that it is Meccan. However, some scholars excepted from it: ﴿They will ask you about the soul﴾ [al-Isra': 85]; the verse ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra': 73] up to His saying ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ [al-Isra': 81]; the verse ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered﴾ [al-Isra': 88] and what follows; His saying ﴿And We did not make the vision﴾ [al-Isra': 60] and what follows; and His saying ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [al-Isra': 107], on the basis of what they mentioned concerning the occasions of their revelation. The discussion of this will come, God willing. Its verses number one hundred and eleven.

[p-3883]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[1] ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾

By His saying ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ He glorifies Himself, declares His lofty essence free of what does not befit His majesty, and magnifies His station for His power over what no one other than Him can do; there is no god but Him. As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, it means: He caused him to journey from it by night. The word (asra) has the same meaning as (sara), one says: asraahu, and asra bihi, and sara bihi. The hamza in (asra) is not for transitivity, which is why it takes the preposition bi. Some scholars distinguished between asra and sara by saying that (asra) carries intensification, to indicate speed in travel, and for this reason it was preferred over (sara).

The isra' is travel through the whole night, like asra. So His saying ﴿by night﴾ is either for emphasis, or for abstraction from some restrictions, like the expression "asaftu maramahu" (I fulfilled his need), although (is'af) means fulfilling a need. Or it is to draw attention to the fact that this is the intended point of mention. Al-Nasir (Ibn al-Munayyir) gave this preference in his "al-Intisaf," saying: A parallel to the singular use of one of what the expression indicates, when its meaning is implicitly intended for something else, is His saying: ﴿Do not take two gods; He is but one God﴾ [al-Nahl: 51]. The word that carries the dual indicates both the dual and the category, and likewise the singular does. So it was intended to draw attention to the fact that one of the two meanings, namely the dual, is intended and sought. Likewise, awakening was intended, since the oneness of God is the aim in His saying ﴿He is but one God﴾ [al-Nahl: 51]. Had He limited Himself to saying "He is but a god," it would have suggested that the important point was affirming divinity for Him, whereas the purpose of the statement is nothing but affirming His oneness.

[p-3884]

It has also been said: the secret of His saying ﴿by night﴾ is to indicate the shortness of the time during which the journey and return took place; that is, it occurred in part of the night. This is drawn from its indefiniteness. It is reported from Sibawayh that when "the night" and "the day" are definite, they serve as a standard for generality, so one does not say "I stayed awake the night" while meaning an hour of it, unless one intends exaggeration. In contrast, the indefinite form does not convey that. Since the verse departed from the definite form here, it is known that he did not intend the whole of the night for the journey, and this is what is meant by partiality. Some scholars allowed that (asra) may derive from (sarah), which is a wide land; its root is from the waw, asra like ajbal and atham, meaning: he took him through a wide land. But this is a strange reading. In specifying the night there is an announcement of its excellence, because it is the time of secrecy, intimate conversation, and the highest manifestation, and for this reason most of his worship ﷺ was by night. By ﴿His servant﴾ is meant the seal of His prophets, Muhammad (ﷺ). In mentioning him with the title of servanthood, together with the attribution to the pronoun of majesty, there is honor, elevation, and an indication of his being singled out by Him, Mighty and Majestic, and of his submission to His commands, which is not hidden.

The word "servant" (abd) linguistically means a human being in general, and a slave; "servanthood" (ubudiyyah) means humility, submission, bondage, and obedience, like "ibadah" and "ubudah."

Ibn al-Qayyim said in "Tariq al-Hijratayn": The most perfect of creation is the most perfect in servanthood, and the greatest in witnessing, because of his poverty, his need, and his dependence on his Lord, and his not being self-sufficient even for the blink of an eye. For this reason one of his supplications (ﷺ) was: "Set right for me all my affairs, and do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye, nor to anyone of Your creation." Then he said: For this reason he was the closest of creation to God in means, the greatest in standing before Him, and the highest in rank with Him, because he perfected the station of servanthood and poverty. He used to say: "O people! I do not like that you raise me above my station; I am only a servant." He also used to say: "Do not exalt me as the Christians exalted Christ, son of Mary; I am only a servant, so say: the servant of God and His messenger." God, glory be to Him, mentioned him with the mark of servanthood in his most noble stations: the station of the isra', the station of the call, and the station of challenge (tahaddi). He said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾, and He said: ﴿And when the servant of God stood calling upon Him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19], and He said: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]. In the hadith of intercession, Christ says to them: "Go to Muhammad, a servant whose past and future sins God has forgiven." So he attained that through the perfection of his servanthood to God, and through the perfection of God's forgiveness for him. End of quotation.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ means the Sacred Mosque of Mecca, may it be honored. It was called "haram" (sacred), like its land, because it is not lawful to violate it by fighting within it, nor by hunting its game, nor by cutting its trees or its herbage. His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿to al-Masjid al-Aqsa﴾ is the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which was known as the Temple of Solomon, because he is the one who built it and erected it. And ﴿al-Aqsa﴾ means "the farthest." It was so named because of its distance from Mecca. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾ means its sides are blessed with the blessings of religion and of the world, because that blessed land is the dwelling place of the prophets, the descent of their revelation, and the place where crops and fruits grow. Thus divine blessing encompassed it from all its sides. Its blessing is therefore multiplied, both because it is in a blessed land and because it is one of the greatest mosques of God, Exalted is He, and mosques are the houses of God; and because it is the place of worship and dwelling of the prophets and the descent of revelation upon them, so the blessings and auspiciousness of those prophets were also bestowed upon it.

It has been said concerning the special features of al-Aqsa: it is the place of worship of the earlier prophets, the path of the seal of the prophets, and the site of his ascent to the lofty heavens and the highest witnessing. It is a house that God exalted in the detailed verses, and in which the four revealed books were recited. For its sake God held back the sun for Joshua so that it did not set, to make easier its conquest for those who were promised it and who were near to it. It is the qiblah for prayer in both religions, and at the beginning of Islam after the two migrations. It is the first of the two qiblahs, the second of the two mosques, and the third of the two sanctuaries. Journeys are not undertaken, after the two mosques, except to it, [p-3886] and the fingers are not interlocked, after the two places, except upon it. End of quotation. Among its virtues is what Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) narrated from Ibn Amr, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When Solomon built Bayt al-Maqdis, he asked his Lord three things. He gave him two, and I hope He gave him the third."
He asked Him for a judgment that would coincide with His judgment, and He gave it to him.
He asked Him for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, and He gave it to him.
And he asked that whoever left his house intending only to pray in this mosque, meaning Bayt al-Maqdis, would come out of his sins as on the day his mother bore him.
The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And we hope that God has granted him that."

It is also reported that Ibn Umar, when he entered it, would not drink its water, out of devotion to the purpose of prayer.

Al-Shirazi said in "Ara'is al-Bayan": The beginning of the mi'raj was the journey to al-Aqsa, because there are the great signs from the lights of His manifestation, Exalted is He, to the spirits and bodies of the prophets. There, near it, are Mount Sinai, Mount Zaytha, and the stations of Abraham, Moses, and Jesus on those mountains, places of the unveiling of the Truth. For this reason He said: ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾. End of quotation.

The shift in ﴿We have blessed﴾ is for glorifying what was mentioned, because the act of the great is great, especially when it is expressed in a form of glorification. The general point is to energize the listeners.

[p-3887]

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that We might show him of Our signs﴾ points to the wisdom of the isra'. That is: so that We might show Muhammad (ﷺ) of Our great signs, among which is his journey in a moment of the night over a distance of a month, the witnessing of Bayt al-Maqdis, the appearance of the prophets to him, and his standing at their exalted stations.

It has been said: God, Exalted is He, willed to show him sensory signs after He had shown him intellectual signs, because sensory signs are more decisive in removing doubt and dispelling whisperings than intellectual ones; for no one doubts what is known through the senses and direct observation. Doubt and whisperings may arise regarding intellectual matters, since no one doubts his own self that he is himself. So He, Mighty and Majestic, willed to show His messenger sensory signs, which would draw the fair-minded to accept them, believe in them, and acknowledge his prophethood; for that is not the work of magic, nor fabrication, nor the fables of the ancients. This is what can be derived from "al-Ta'wilat" of Abu Mansur.

How excellent is what Ibn Ishaq said: His journey (ﷺ) and what was mentioned of it was a trial and a testing, and a matter from the affairs of God in His power and dominion. In it is a lesson for people of understanding, guidance, mercy, and steadfastness for whoever believes in God and affirms. It was one of the affairs of God, Glory be to Him and Exalted, with certainty. So God, Glory be to Him and Exalted, took him by night as He willed, that He might show him of His signs what He willed, until he witnessed what he witnessed of His great affair and dominion, and of His power by which He does what He wills. End of quotation.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ means: All-Hearing of the words and deeds of His servants, so nothing is hidden from Him on earth or in heaven.

Remarks:

First: This verse establishes the isra', which is the Prophet's (ﷺ) night journey to Bayt al-Maqdis. As for the ascent to the heavens and to what is above the Throne, this verse does not indicate it. [p-3888] Some have derived it from the beginning of Surat al-Najm, and the discussion of that is there.

Second: Most scholars held that the isra' took place after the beginning of the prophethood (mab'ath), and that it was one year before his migration. This was said by al-Zuhri, Ibn Sa'd, and others. al-Nawawi affirmed it decisively, and Ibn Hazm exaggerated and reported a consensus (ijma') on it. He said: It was in Rajab in the twelfth year of prophethood.

In "Insan al-Uyun" it is stated that this night was the night of the seventeenth. It was also said: the twenty-seventh of Rabi' al-Awwal; it was also said: the night of the twenty-ninth of Ramadan; it was also said: the twenty-seventh of Rabi' al-Akhir; and it was said: it was in Rajab. The last of these was chosen by the hafiz Abd al-Ghani al-Maqdisi, who said: The people act upon it. And God knows best.

Part 2 of 4 of the commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 17, verse 1.

Third: In Zad al-Ma'ad by Ibn al-Qayyim: the Isra' occurred once. It was also said that it occurred twice: once while awake and once in a dream. The proponents of this view seem to have wanted to reconcile the hadith of Sharik, with his words "then I awoke" (thumma istayqadtu), with the other narrations. Some said: rather, it occurred twice, once before the revelation, based on the words in the hadith of Sharik ("and that was before he was given revelation"), and once after the revelation, as the other hadiths indicate. Others said: rather, it occurred three times: once before the revelation and twice after it. All of this is confusion (khabt), and it is the method of the weak literalists (Zahiriyyah) among the transmitters, who, whenever they find in the story a wording that contradicts the context of some of the narrations, make it a separate occurrence. Thus, whenever the narrations conflict for them, they multiply the events. The correct view, upon which the leading transmitters (a'immat al-naql) agree, is that the Isra' occurred once, in Makkah, after the Prophethood (ba'thah). How strange it is about those who claimed that it happened repeatedly! How could they suppose that each time the prayers were prescribed at fifty, then he would go back and forth between his Lord and Musa until they became five, then he would say: "I have established My obligation and lightened it for My servants," and then he would return it in the second occurrence to fifty and then reduce it ten by ten?!

Fourth: Qadi 'Iyad, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Shifa': The predecessors (al-salaf) and scholars differed over whether the Isra' was with his spirit (ruh) or his body (jasad), in three positions. One group held that it was a journey of the spirit alone and that it was a dream vision, while agreeing that the visions of the Prophets are true and a form of revelation. Mu'awiyah took this view, and it is related from al-Hasan (though the well-known position from him is the opposite), and Muhammad ibn Ishaq alluded to it. Their proof is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you﴾ [al-Isra': 60], and what they related from 'A'ishah: "I did not miss the body of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ," and his words "While I was sleeping," and the words of Anas: (while he was sleeping in al-Masjid al-Haram), and he mentioned the story, then said at its end: (then he awoke and I was in al-Masjid al-Haram).

Most of the predecessors and Muslims held that it was a journey with the body and while awake. This is the truth, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir, Anas, Hudhayfah, 'Umar, Abu Hurayrah, Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, Abu Habbah al-Badri, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Shihab, Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Masruq, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jurayj. It is also the indication of 'A'ishah's statement. It is the view of al-Tabari, Ibn Hanbal and a great multitude of Muslims. It is the view of most later jurists, hadith scholars, theologians and exegetes.

Some said: The Isra' was with the body, while awake, to Bayt al-Maqdis, and to the heaven with the spirit. They argued from His words: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾, where He made al-Masjid al-Aqsa the end point of the journey in which the wonder lies, in the magnitude of power and in praise of the honouring of the Prophet and the showing of his dignity through the journey to it. These said: If the journey had been with his body beyond al-Masjid al-Aqsa, it would have been mentioned, and it would have been more eloquent in praise.

Then these two groups differed over whether he prayed in Bayt al-Maqdis or not. In the hadith of Anas and others, he prayed there. Hudhayfah denied this and said: "By Allah! They did not leave the back of the Buraq until they returned."

Then Qadi 'Iyad said: The truth in this matter, and the sound view, Allah willing, is that it was a journey with both body and spirit throughout the whole story. The verse indicates this, as do the sound reports and sound reasoning. One does not depart from the apparent meaning and the literal sense to figurative interpretation except when it is impossible, and there is no impossibility in a journey with his body in the state of wakefulness. For if it had been a dream, he would have said "with the spirit of His servant" and not "with His servant." And His words: ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. Had it been a dream, there would have been no sign or miracle in it, the disbelievers would not have deemed it unlikely nor denied it, and the weak among those who had embraced Islam would not have apostatised or been tested by it, since such a thing in dreams is not denied. Rather, they did not react in that way except because they knew that his report was about his body and his state of wakefulness, as mentioned in the hadith: his praying with the Prophets in Bayt al-Maqdis in the narration of Anas (or in the heaven) as others narrated, and the mention of Jibril coming to him with the Buraq, and the account of the Mi'raj and the opening of the heaven, when it is said: "Who is with you?" and he says: "Muhammad." And his meeting the Prophets there, their account with him, their welcoming him, and his position regarding the prescription of prayer and his returning with Musa about it.

In some of these reports: "Then Jibril, took my hand and ascended with me to the heaven," up to his words: "Then he ascended with me until I reached a level where I could hear the scratching of the pens," and that he reached Sidrat al-Muntaha, and that he entered Paradise and saw in it what he mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was a vision of the eye that the Prophet ﷺ saw, not a dream vision.

And from al-Hasan regarding it: "While I was sleeping in al-Hijr, Jibril came to me and prodded me with his heel, so I got up and sat, but I saw nothing, so I returned to my bed." He mentioned this three times, and in the third he said: "Then he took me by the arms and dragged me to the door of the mosque, and there was an animal," and he mentioned the account of the Buraq.

From Umm Hani: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not taken on the Isra' except while he was in my house that night. He prayed the late night prayer ('isha' al-akhirah) and slept among us. When it was near dawn we woke the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and when he had prayed the dawn prayer and we had prayed, he said: 'O Umm Hani! I prayed with you the late night prayer, as you saw, in this valley. Then I came to Bayt al-Maqdis and prayed in it, then I prayed the morning prayer with you now as you see.'" This is clear that it was with his body.

From Abu Bakr (through the narration of Shaddad ibn Aws from him) that he "said to the Prophet ﷺ on the night of his Isra': 'I looked for you, O Messenger of Allah, last night in your place and did not find you.' He replied: 'Jibril carried me to al-Masjid al-Aqsa.'"

From 'Umar, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I prayed on the night I was taken on the Isra' at the front of the mosque, then I entered the Rock." These explicit statements are apparent and not impossible, so they are taken in their apparent sense.

From Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The roof of my house was opened while I was in Makkah, Jibril descended, then took my hand and ascended with me."

From Anas: "I came, and they set off with me to Zamzam." From Abu Hurayrah: "I saw myself in al-Hijr while Quraysh were asking me about my journey, and they asked me about things I had not memorised, so I was distressed with a distress I had never felt like before, then Allah raised it for me and I was looking at it." Similar is reported from Jabir.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, related in the hadith of the Isra' from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Then I returned to Khadijah and I had not moved from her side."

Then Qadi 'Iyad said (refuting the arguments of those who said it was a dream): They argued from His words: ﴿And We did not make the vision﴾ [al-Isra': 60], calling it "vision" (ru'ya). We say: His words ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ refute this, since one does not say "took by night" (asra) of a dream.

And His words: ﴿a trial for the people﴾ [al-Isra': 60] confirm that it was a vision of the eye and a journey of a person, since there is no trial in a dream, and no one would deny it, for everyone sees the like of that in his dream: being in distant regions within a single hour. Moreover, the exegetes differed regarding this verse. Some held that it was revealed concerning the story of Hudaybiyah and what occurred to people's minds because of it. It was said other than this.

As for their claim that he called it a dream in the hadith, and his words in another hadith: "between the sleeper and the waker" (bayna al-na'im wal-yaqzan), and his words also: "while he was sleeping," and "then I awoke," there is no proof in these: it is possible that the first arrival of the Angel to him was while he was sleeping, or the beginning of his dream and the Isra' with him while he was sleeping. There is nothing in the hadith that he was asleep throughout the whole story, except what indicates it: "Then I awoke while I was in al-Masjid al-Haram." Perhaps his words "I awoke" mean "I arose in the morning," or he woke from another sleep after reaching his house. This is indicated by the fact that his night journey did not last the whole night, but only part of it. It may be that his words "I awoke while I was in al-Masjid al-Haram" were due to what had overwhelmed him of the wonders he witnessed of the realm (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, and what entered his heart from witnessing the Exalted Assembly, and the great signs of his Lord he saw. So he did not come to himself and return to the human state until he was in al-Masjid al-Haram.

A third possibility: that his sleep and waking were literal according to the apparent meaning of the wording, but he was taken on the journey with his body while his heart was present, and the visions of the Prophets are true. Their eyes sleep but their hearts do not sleep.

Some of the people of the (mystical) allusions (ashab al-isharat) have inclined to something similar to this. He said: Closing his eyes was so that nothing of the sensible objects would distract him from Allah, and this does not apply at the time of his praying with the Prophets, and perhaps he had states in this journey.

A fourth possibility: that sleep here refers to the posture of a sleeper, i.e. lying down. This is reinforced by his words in the narration of 'Abd ibn Humayd from Hammam: "While I was sleeping," and perhaps he said "lying down"; and in the narration of Hudbah from him: "While I was in al-Hatim," and perhaps he said "in al-Hijr lying down." And his words in the other narration: "between the sleeper and the waker," so he called his posture sleep because the posture of a sleeper was the usual one.

Some said that these additions concerning sleep, the mention of the splitting of the chest, and the drawing near of the Lord, which occur in this hadith, are only from the narration of Sharik from Anas. Therefore they are rejected from his narration. The words of 'Iyad end here. There remains a remainder of it; whoever wishes may consult it.

The fifth point: the total of the opinions on the Isra' and the Mi'raj, as Ibn al-Qayyim relates them in (Zad al-Ma'ad), is six. The first is that it occurred with his spirit and body, which is the view they declared sound. It was also said that it was a dream. It was also said that one may say "he was taken by night" (usriya bihi) without saying it was while awake or in a dream. It was also said that the journey to Bayt al-Maqdis was while awake and the ascent to the heavens was in a dream. It was also said that the journey happened twice, once awake and once in a dream. And it was said that he was taken by night three times. All of this occurred after the Prophethood (al-ba'th), by consensus. As for what occurred in the hadith of Sharik, that this happened before he received revelation (qabla an yuha ilayhi), it was said that this is an error. It was also said that the "revelation" here is restricted and is not the absolute revelation which is the beginning of prophethood. The intended meaning is: before he received revelation concerning the journey, so he was taken by night suddenly without prior notice. We have already mentioned that the majority transmitted from 'A'isha, Mu'awiya and al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with them) that it was a dream vision. Likewise Ibn Jarir related it from Hudhayfa (may Allah be pleased with him). (p-3893) However, Ibn al-Qayyim drew attention to a subtle and unusual point. He said, may Allah have mercy on him: Ibn Ishaq related from 'A'isha and Mu'awiya that they both said: the journey was only with his spirit, and his body was not lost. Something similar has been related from al-Hasan al-Basri. But it should be known that there is a difference between saying "the journey was a dream" and saying "it was with his spirit without his body." And between the two there is a great difference. 'A'isha and Mu'awiya did not say it was a dream; they only said: he was taken by night with his spirit, and his body was not lost. And there is a difference between the two matters. For what the sleeper sees may be parables struck for known realities in perceptible forms, so he sees as if he was taken up to the heavens, or taken to Makkah and the regions of the earth, while his spirit did not ascend and did not go. Rather, the angel of dreams struck the example for him. Those who said the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken up are of two groups. One group said: he was taken up with his spirit and his body. Another group said: he was taken up with his spirit, and his body was not lost. These did not mean that the Mi'raj was a dream. They meant that the spirit itself was taken by night and taken up in reality, and it engaged in the same kind of activity it engages in after departure, in its ascent through the heavens, heaven by heaven, until it reaches the seventh heaven, and it stands before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He commands in it what He wills, then it descends to the earth. What was granted to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of the Isra' was more complete than what the spirit attains at departure. It is known that this is a matter beyond what the sleeper sees. But since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in a station of breaking customary norms, to the extent that his chest was split while he was alive and did not feel pain, so likewise the very spirit of his blessed self was taken up in reality without death. As for anyone other than him (ﷺ), the very spirit cannot attain ascent to the heavens except after death and departure. The prophets' spirits settled there only after their bodies departed. The spirit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ascended there while he was alive and then returned. After his death it settled in the Highest Companion (al-Rafiq al-A'la) with the spirits of the prophets. Nevertheless, it has a supervision over the body, and illumination and attachment to it, such that it returns the greeting to whoever greets him. By this attachment Musa was seen standing and praying in his grave, and he was seen in the sixth heaven. It is known that Musa was not taken up from his grave and then returned to it. Rather, that was the station of his spirit and its settling, while his grave is the station of his body and its settling until the Day of the Return of spirits to their bodies. So he was seen praying in his grave, and he was seen in the sixth heaven. Just as he (ﷺ) is in the highest place in the Highest Companion, settled there, while his body in his tomb is not lost. When one who greets him sends greeting, Allah returns his spirit to him until he returns the greeting, and he has not departed from the Exalted Assembly. Whoever has a dense perception and a coarse nature, unable to grasp this, let him look at the sun in the height of its place, its connection, its effect on the earth, and the life of plants and animals through it. This is so, and the matter of the spirit is above this. For it has a matter and the bodies have a matter. This fire is in its place, yet its heat affects a body far from it. Yet the connection and attachment between the spirit and the body is stronger, more complete and more perfect than that. So the matter of the spirit is higher than that and more subtle.

A poet said:
"Say to the eyes that are diseased: beware of looking at the light of the sun, and so veil yourselves in the darkness of the nights."

The words of Ibn al-Qayyim have ended.

Al-'Allama Sa'di (in Hawashi al-Baydawi) said: the Mi'raj with his spirit while awake, which is what Ibn al-Qayyim pointed to, is also a breach of custom.

Al-'Allama al-Qunawi objected to him: it is a kind of contemplation and detachment, and what the Sufis hold is invalid, because it is far beyond that. Rather, it is other than that, as has been made clear before. In sum, what most understood from the statements of 'A'isha, Mu'awiya, Hudhayfa and al-Hasan is that it was a dream vision. What Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned, that it was a journey with the spirit, the transmitted wording from them may bear.

A similar statement is that of some who said: that was a miraculous matter (amr i'jazi). The reality is that it was a spiritual unveiling (kashf ruhani). They have also established, regarding the non-impossibility of its being while awake with both spirit and body, that the Creator of the world is capable of all possible things. And the occurrence of motion reaching such extreme speed in his blessed body (ﷺ) is possible. Therefore it is necessary that He, exalted, be capable of it. And the most that can be said is that it is contrary to custom. All miracles are like that. In (al-'Aqa'id al-Nasafiyya) and its commentaries: the tearing and rejoining of the heavens is permissible, because all bodies are alike in being composed of indivisible atoms (jawahir fardah), so what is valid for one is valid for another. Elemental bodies are capable of tearing and rejoining, and likewise celestial bodies. And Allah, exalted, is capable of all possible things. So He is capable of tearing in the heavens, because it is possible in them. In al-Razi there are other proofs, so look at them.

It is mentioned in the book (Izhar al-Haqq) that some of the People of the Book disputed about the Mi'raj, and they were rebuked: that the ascent of a physical elemental body to the spheres is declared by the Torah that they possess concerning (Akhnukh). It was related that he was taken up alive to the heaven so that he would not see death, as in the fifth chapter of the Book of Genesis. And it is declared in the ascent of (Elijah) in the second chapter of the Book of Kings. And in the Gospel of Mark, in the sixteenth chapter, there is explicit mention of the raising of the Messiah (peace be upon him) to heaven. End of quotation.

I say: Akhnukh is Idris (peace be upon him), the one mentioned in His saying, exalted: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾ [Maryam: 57]. Elijah (Ilya) is a prophet who was sent to Ahab, one of the disbelieving Jewish kings, who publicized the worship of Ba'l and other idols in Samaria. It is now called Sebastiya, from the region of the Holy Land. They claimed that remarkable marvels appeared at the hand of Elijah, and that he killed the servants of Ba'l and demolished his altar, until he was raised in a chariot of fire and horses of fire toward the heavens, from the side of the river Jordan in the plains of Jericho, witnessed by his successor, the prophet Elisha (al-Yasha') after him. So it is in the History of the Holy Book. And (Ilya) is Ilyas, and (al-Yasha') is al-Yasa', both mentioned in the Glorious Qur'an.

The first was alluded to in Surat al-Saffat in His saying, exalted: ﴿And indeed Ilyas was among the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat: 123] ﴿When he said to his people: Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [al-Saffat: 124] ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l and abandon the best of creators﴾ [al-Saffat: 125] ﴿Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers﴾ [al-Saffat: 126].

The sixth point: it has been said that the Masjid al-Aqsa at the time of the Isra' was in ruins, as attested by history. This is because Sulayman (peace be upon him) built it over the place of the Rock, then it fell into ruin, and the refuse of the city was thrown onto the Rock out of spite toward the Jews. It remained so until Amir al-Mu'minin 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) conquered Jerusalem. See (Tarikh Abi al-Fida') and others. How then was the name "mosque" applied to it? I answer: a mosque while it is being demolished is still called a mosque, in consideration of what it was and what it was established for, just as the name "mosque" was applied to the Sacred Precinct of Makkah, though it was not a mosque at that time. It was only a house for idols.

But Ibrahim and Isma'il, when they built the Ka'ba for the true worship, just as Sulayman built this temple for it, it was called a mosque on this basis. Or it may be said: the name "mosque" was applied to both of them to point to what their affair would result in, namely that they would be two mosques for the Muslims.

The seventh point: concerning the comparison between the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) and the Night of the Isra'. Imam Taqi al-Din Ahmad Ibn Taymiyya (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about a man who said: the Night of the Isra' is better than the Night of Power, and another said: rather the Night of Power is better. Which of them is correct?

He answered: As for the one who said the Night of the Isra' is better than the Night of Power: if he meant that the night in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken by night and its like each year is better for the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) than the Night of Power, such that its standing in prayer and supplication is better than in the Night of Power, then this is false. No one among the Muslims has said it, and it is known to be false by necessity from the religion of Islam. This is so if the Night of the Isra' were known by its specific identity. How then, when no known proof has established its month, nor its decade, nor its specific night? Rather, the reports concerning it are discontinuous and conflicting, and none of them is conclusive. Nor has it been legislated for the Muslims to single out the night believed to be the Night of the Isra' with standing in prayer or anything else. Unlike the Night of Power, for it has been established in the two Sahihs from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Power in faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven." And in the two Sahihs from him: (p-3897) "Seek the Night of Power in the last ten nights of Ramadan." And Allah, glorified is He, has informed that it is better than a thousand months, for in it the Qur'an was sent down.

And if he meant that the specific night in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken by night, and in which he received what he did not receive in any other, without it being legislated to single it out with standing in prayer or worship, then this is correct. But when Allah grants His Prophet (ﷺ) a virtue in a place or time, it does not follow that that time and place must be better than all places and times. This is supposing that a proof has established that Allah's blessing upon His Prophet on the Night of the Isra' was greater than His blessing upon him by sending down the Qur'an on the Night of Power, and other blessings which He bestowed upon him. And speech on such a matter requires knowledge of the realities of the affair and the measures of blessings, which are not known except through revelation. And it is not permissible for anyone to speak about them without knowledge.

Not a single one of the Muslims is reported to have singled out the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey) as more virtuous than other nights, least of all the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr). Nor did the Companions and the Followers who came after them in good conduct intend to single out the night of the Isra' for any matter or mention it for that purpose. For this reason, no one knows which night it was. Although the Isra' is among the greatest of the virtues of the Prophet (ﷺ), the time and place of it were not established as an object of legislated worship. Rather, the Cave of Hira', where revelation began and where he used to seek seclusion before prophethood, was not visited by him or by any of his Companions after prophethood during his stay in Makkah. The day on which revelation was sent down was not singled out for worship or anything else, nor was the place where revelation began, nor the time. Whoever singles out places and times for acts of worship on his own account because of this or similar matters is of the same kind as the People of the Book, who made the times of the events of the life of the Messiah into occasions and rites of worship, such as the Day of the Birth, the Day of Baptism, and other events of his life.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab saw a group hurrying toward a place to pray in. He said: "What is this?" They said: "A place where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed." He said: "Do you wish to take the traces of your prophets as places of worship? Those before you were destroyed by this. Whoever is overtaken by the prayer there, let him pray; otherwise, let him pass on."

Some people have said: the night of the Isra' is, with respect to the Prophet (ﷺ), more excellent than the Night of Decree, while the Night of Decree is more excellent for the Ummah than the night of the Isra'. Thus this night is more excellent for them (the Ummah), and the night of the Isra' is more excellent for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). End of quotation. This was transmitted by ash-Shams Ibn al-Qayyim (in Zad al-Ma'ad).

Eighth: Ash-Shams Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Ma'ad: The Companions differed over whether the Prophet (ﷺ) saw his Lord that night or not. It is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he saw his Lord. It is also authentically reported from him that he said: "He saw Him with his heart." It is authentically reported from 'A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud that they denied this and said that the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13] ﴿at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 14] refer only to Jibril. It is authentically reported from Abu Dharr that he asked him: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "Light; how could I see Him?!" That is, the light stood between me and seeing it. As he said in another wording: "I saw light." 'Uthman ibn Sa'id ad-Darimi related a consensus of the Companions that he did not see Him.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his soul, said: The statement of Ibn 'Abbas that he saw Him is not contradictory to this, nor is his saying that he saw Him with his heart. It is authentically reported from him that he said: "I saw my Lord, blessed and exalted." But this was not during the Isra'; it was in Madinah when he was delayed from them at the dawn prayer. Then he informed them about seeing his Lord, blessed and exalted, that night in his dream. On this basis Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, built his view and said: "Yes, he saw Him truly, for the dreams of the prophets are true, without doubt." But Ahmad did not say that he saw Him with the eyes of his head. Whoever relates that from him has erred regarding him. Ahmad said at one time: "He saw Him," and at another time: "He saw Him with his heart." So two narrations were reported from him, and a third was reported, which is an interpretation by some of his companions that he saw Him with the eyes of his head. The texts of Ahmad are extant and contain nothing of that. As for the statement of Ibn 'Abbas that he saw Him with his heart twice: if its basis is the words of Allah, ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [al-Najm: 11], followed by ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13], and this is apparently its basis, then it is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that this one seen was Jibril, whom he saw twice in his original form in which he was created. This statement of Ibn 'Abbas is the basis of Imam Ahmad's statement: "He saw Him with his heart." And Allah knows best.

Ninth: The hafiz Abu al-Khattab 'Umar ibn Dihyah said in his book "at-Tanwir fi Mawlid as-Siraj al-Munir", after mentioning the hadith of the Isra' through the route of Anas: "The narrations of the hadith of the Isra' have been reported by mass transmission from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Dharr, Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa'id, Ibn 'Abbas, Shaddad ibn Aws, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Qurt, Abu Habbah and Abu Layla al-Ansariyyayn, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Jabir, Hudhayfah, Buraydah, Abu Ayyub, Abu Umamah, Samurah ibn Jundub, Abu al-Hamra', Suhayb al-Rumi, Umm Hani', 'A'ishah, and Asma', the two daughters of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with them all. Some of them related it in full and some abridged it, as it occurs in the Masanid. Even if the narration of some of them does not meet the condition of soundness, the hadith of the Isra' has been agreed upon by the Muslims, and the heretics and the atheists have turned away from it." End of quotation.

Ar-Razi related from some of the Mu'tazilah their rejection of sentences in it, which he cited, and which were difficult for them to comprehend. In reality, there is no difficulty in them, praise be to Allah, the Exalted. But they and those like them, whose concern with the science of hadith is weak and whose attention has been dominated by rational sciences, have thereby missed much good. There is nothing in the authentic hadiths that contradicts the event that occurred or the reality in any way; the firmly grounded scholars know this. And above every possessor of knowledge is One, All-Knowing.

Among those who related it from the Companions, besides those mentioned earlier, are Sahl ibn Sa'd, 'Abd Allah ibn Hawalah al-Azdi, 'Abd Allah ibn As'ad ibn Zurarah, Abu al-Darda', and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar. As for those among the Followers who related it without a Companion in the chain (mursal), they are many, among them: al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn, peace be upon them both, Ka'b, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, 'Urwah, Sufyan ath-Thawri, al-Walid ibn Muslim, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, and others, as is known from consulting "ad-Durr al-Manthur" of the hafiz as-Suyuti.

As for its routes in the Two Sahihs, the hafiz Ibn Hajar said in "al-Fath": they revolve around Anas ibn Malik, with differences among his students regarding him. Qatadah related it from him, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, and there is no hadith of the Mi'raj more authentic than it. az-Zuhri related it from him, from Abu Dharr. Shurayk ibn Abi Namir and Thabit al-Bunani related it from him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) directly without an intermediary. Each of them has in his version from him what is not in the other's. And His, the Exalted's, statement:

The discourse concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[2–3] ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying], "Take not other than Me as a Disposer of affairs (wakil).﴾ ﴿[You are] the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:3]

﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying], "Take not other than Me as a Disposer of affairs (wakil).﴾ ﴿[You are] the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:3]

Ibn Kathir said: When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He had carried His servant Muhammad ﷺ by night, He linked it with the mention of Moses, His servant, messenger and interlocutor (kalim). He, exalted is He, often pairs the mention of Moses and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, and the mention of the Torah and the Qur'an.

Al-Razi said: When God, exalted is He, mentioned in the first verse His honouring of Muhammad ﷺ by carrying him by night, He mentioned in this verse that He honoured Moses, peace and blessings be upon him, before him with the Scripture that He gave him.

Al-Shihab said in (al-'Inayah): The verse of the Night Journey is followed by this one by way of digression (istitrad), on the ground that Moses, peace and blessings be upon him, was given the Torah through his journey to Mount Sinai, which was like his ascension (mi'raj), for speech (taklim) was realised there, and he was honoured with the name "the Interlocutor," with the difference between the two Scriptures and the two who received them being implicitly included. If you wish, compare: ﴿Who carried His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra' 17:1] with: ﴿And We gave Moses﴾; and: ﴿a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾ with: ﴿guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra' 17:9]. The waw is either resumptive (istि'nafiyyah) or conjunctive, connecting to the clause "Glory be to Him who carried [His servant] by night," etc., not to "carried" (asra), due to its remoteness and its artificiality. The pronoun in (wa-ja'alnahu) refers either to the Scripture or to Moses, and (li-Bani Isra'il) is related to (huda) or to (ja'alnahu), and the lam is causal (ta'lil).

As for His saying: ﴿Take not other than Me as a Disposer of affairs (wakil)﴾, meaning: a protector and an object of worship to whom you entrust your affairs, because He, exalted is He, sent down to every prophet He sent that he should worship Him alone, with no partner. It has been read: {Alla yattakhidhu} (p-3901) with the ya' (third person), by omitting the lam of causation; the implied sense being: We made it a guidance so that they would not take. It has also been read with the ta' (second person), and in this there are three aspects:

First: that (an) is in the sense of (ayy), explanatory of what the Scripture contains of command and prohibition.

Second: that (an) is superfluous, i.e., "We said: Do not take."

Third: that (la) is superfluous, and the sense is: lest you take. The wakil is the one entrusted with affairs, i.e., the one to whom affairs are committed, namely the Lord. So (fa'il) is in the sense of (maf'ul). (Dun) is in the sense of (ghayr). (Min) is either superfluous or partitive.

His saying: ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ [al-Isra' 17:3] is in the accusative either by specification (ikhtisas) or by address (nida'). In it is an arousing and an alerting to the favour and bounty bestowed upon them in saving their forefathers from drowning by carrying them with Noah in the ark. It also hints at the reason for the prohibition, as if it were said: Do not associate anything with Him, for He is the Bestower of favour upon you and the One who delivers you from hardships, and you are weak, in need of His gentleness. In the expression "offspring" (dhurriyyah), which is commonly used for children and women, there is a complete appropriateness to what has been mentioned. He mentioned their being carried in the ark to indicate that they had then no disposer of affairs upon whom to rely other than Him. His saying: ﴿a grateful servant﴾ [al-Isra' 17:3] means: for his knowledge of God's blessings and his employing them in the manner that is fitting. In it is a hint that his salvation and that of those with him was by the blessing of his gratitude, and an exhortation to his offspring to follow his example. It has been said that this is a digression. His exalted saying:

(p-3902)

[2–3] ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying], "Take not other than Me as a Disposer of affairs (wakil).﴾ ﴿[You are] the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:3]

(p-3902)

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[4-5] "And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture: 'You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice, and you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance.' So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they went through the homes; and it was a promise fulfilled." [Al-Isra: 5]

"And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture" – i.e., in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz); meaning, We judged therein: "You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice" – meaning the land of Palestine, Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which Allah has blessed around. Corruption (al-ifsad) is by disbelief and sins.

Al-Samin said: In the transitivity of "qadayna" (We decreed) with "ila" (to), there is an implication of the meaning of "anfadhna" (We carried out/sent forth), i.e., We sent forth to them the decree that is binding. The object of the decree is omitted, i.e., [it concerns] their corruption. His saying "You will surely cause corruption" is the answer to an omitted oath, emphasizing the meaning of the decree; or it is the answer to His saying "And We decreed," since it has been included with the meaning of an oath. From this is the saying of people: "By the decree of Allah, I will surely do such-and-such," so they treat the decree and the destiny as an oath, and they are followed by what follows an oath. "Twice" (marratayn) means two instances of corruption; it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) of "tufsidunna" from its own root, but it was avoided because the dual and plural of the verbal noun is not regular. "And you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance" – i.e., you will surely be haughty and exalt yourselves against obedience to Allah, Exalted is He, or you will surely wrong people.

"So when the promise of the first of them came" – i.e., the promised outcome of the first of the two instances, meaning what they were promised in the first time: the promise of retribution for the first of the two corruptions. "We sent against you servants of Ours of great might" – i.e., possessors of strength and severity in war. "They went through the homes" – they roamed through your dwellings and places for killing, captivity, and plunder. "And it was a promise fulfilled" – i.e., decreed, with no one able to avert it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 17, verses 6–8:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[6–8] ﴿Then We gave back to you the turn of victory over them, and We aided you with wealth and sons, and made you more numerous in manpower.﴾ ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own selves; and if you do evil, it is for them. So when the promise of the Last Time came, they were sent to disgrace your faces and to enter the Masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy completely whatever they had conquered.﴾ [al-Isra' 7] ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy on you; but if you return, We shall return, and We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Isra' 8].

﴿Then We gave back to you the turn of victory over them﴾: that is, after this severe punishment, We returned, upon your repentance, the dominance that had been yours originally, over them. ﴿And We aided you with wealth and sons, and made you more numerous in manpower﴾: that is, in people and kinsmen. (p-3905) Note:

It is related that the Children of Israel had authority in Palestine until the death of Sulayman, peace be upon him. When his son ruled after him, which was about nine hundred years before the Messiah, disorder occurred in his reign that led to the establishment of idol worship. So after five years of his reign, he was quickly punished by the seizing of the kingdom of Egypt over Jerusalem, the plundering of the treasures of its sanctuary (the Masjid al-Aqsa), and the looting of what was in it. When his conduct became corrupt, his people rebelled against him and rejected his obedience. His kingdom split into two parts. One was called the Kingdom of Judah, consisting of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, which remained subject to the son of Sulayman.

The second was called the Kingdom of Israel, consisting of the remaining ten tribes. The first king over the Kingdom of Israel was a man called Jeroboam, who feared that his subjects would return to obedience to the son of Sulayman if they went up to Jerusalem during the festivals to worship God in the Temple and offer their sacrifices there. So he set up two golden calves in his kingdom and ordered his subjects to worship them. He also arranged for them festivals and priests. Severe wars broke out between the kings of these two groups. Among the kings who came between them were some who abandoned idol worship, but the situation did not last long before another king came and restored paganism. The Kingdom of Israel lasted about two hundred and fifty years. At the end of their affair, their sins grew great, so the king of Assyria was empowered over them. He conquered Samaria, their city, and took them captive to Assyria, and the kingdom of the ten tribes came to an end and their name was no longer heard. Then the king of Assyria sent people from his land and settled them in the cities of Samaria to rebuild them together with those who remained of its people. He sent with them a Jewish priest to establish their rites for those who remained. They returned to their polytheism and the worship of idols alongside God, exalted is He. As for the Kingdom of Judah, it remained after the end of the Kingdom of Israel for about twenty years, and toward the end of its days a wicked king arose. Then the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar (Bukhtnassar), marched against him, took a portion of his people captive, and this was the First Captivity.

Then, after that wicked king, his son arose and followed the way of his father. The aforementioned king of Babylon returned against him (p-3906) and took him captive, along with his family, his leaders and a portion of the people, and plundered the Temple. This was the Second Captivity, eight years after the first.

Then there arose among them a king worse than those before him, who was their last king. In his days the aforementioned king of Babylon also besieged Jerusalem, took him captive to Babylon, burned the city and the Temple, and carried off all the people of Judah, except the poor of the land, to Babylon. This was the Third and final Captivity.

Thus this kingdom came to an end, and their stay in Babylon lasted seventy years. Then they were released from captivity, returned to Jerusalem, and renewed its construction and the erection of the Temple. The Jews remained under the domination of the kings of Persia until Alexander the Great appeared, and the Greeks overcame the Persians. Alexander came to Syria, and the Children of Israel came under Greek rule. After Alexander's death, his kingdom was divided into four parts.

Among them was the kingdom of Syria and Egypt. Continuous wars occurred between them. The Israelites, being among them, were at times under the rule of Egypt and at other times under the domination of Syria. During this period, many Jews rejected the Jewish religion and adhered to the religion of the Greeks.

Then the Romans took control of Palestine, and severe wars took place between them and the Jews, which ended in Roman domination over them. They took possession of Jerusalem. Titus, one of their kings, destroyed the Temple down to its foundations, burned the books of the Jews, and their affairs were scattered. They had no kingdom or leadership after him. They claimed that this happened about forty years after the raising of the Messiah. They also claimed that the Temple was later restored and repaired, until Helena, the mother of Constantine, went to al-Quds and built a church over the tomb which the Christians claim is the tomb of the Messiah. She ruined the Temple and ordered that the city's refuse and sweepings be thrown into it, so the place of the Rock became a dunghill. It remained so until Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, came and conquered al-Quds. He ordered it cleaned and built a mosque on its qibla side. Then, when al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik became ruler, he rebuilt it on its old foundation and built the Dome of the Rock.

(p-3907) The details of these events are well known in the books of history. We have not cited what we have cited as an explanation of the verse, because the verse, with its brevity, is sufficient without it. Our explanation of its words is enough for understanding it. However, most of the exegetes touched upon some of the Jewish historical narratives here, so we have selected the best of what the later historians wrote, to clarify their deeds which the noble verses refer to.

We have previously stated, in the commentary on Surat Yusuf, that the Qur'an contains no history in the sense of story and report. Rather, its verses are for lessons that appear within the context of events. For this reason, no story is mentioned in full detail; only the point of the lesson in it is mentioned, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].

(p-3907) The details of these events are well known in the books of history. We have not cited what we have cited as an explanation of the verse, because the verse, with its brevity, is sufficient without it. Our explanation of its words is enough for understanding it. However, most of the exegetes touched upon some of the Jewish historical narratives here, so we have selected the best of what the later historians wrote, to clarify their deeds which the noble verses refer to.

We have previously stated, in the commentary on Surat Yusuf, that the Qur'an contains no history in the sense of story and report. Rather, its verses are for lessons that appear within the context of events. For this reason, no story is mentioned in full detail; only the point of the lesson in it is mentioned, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the excellence of the Noble Revelation by which it surpasses all that was revealed, through His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward.﴾

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ That is: to the condition that is the most upright and soundest of conditions; or to the (religious) community (milla); or to the way (tariqa).

Al-Zamakhshari said: Whichever way you estimate it, you will not find with the affirmation (of the noun) the taste of eloquence that you find with the omission, because of the grandeur that is lost when the described noun is made explicit, the grandeur arising from leaving it vague by omitting it.

﴿and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward﴾ That is: it gives good tidings to those sincere in their faith, who are those who do all righteous deeds and avoid evil deeds, that they will have abundant reward in this world and in the Hereafter.

(p-3908)

And as for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment. ﴿And those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And man supplicates for evil as he supplicates for good, and man has ever been hasty.﴾ [al-Isra'17: 11]

﴿And those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., in the Resurrection and the recompense for deeds: ﴿We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾, i.e., in the Hereafter, which is the punishment of the Fire.

﴿And man supplicates for evil as he supplicates for good﴾ [al-Isra' 17: 11], i.e., like his supplication for good: ﴿and man has ever been hasty﴾ [al-Isra' 17: 11]. Abu al-Su'ud said: The verse is an explanation of the condition of the one who is guided, following the explanation of the condition of the guide, and a showing of the contrast between them. By "man" is meant the species, and the condition of some of its individuals is attributed to it, or He relates his condition at some of his times. So the meaning, according to the first view, is: the Qur'an calls man to the good beyond which there is no good, the great reward, and warns him against the evil beyond which there is no evil, the painful punishment. And he, i.e., some of him, namely the disbeliever, supplicates for himself for what is the evil of the mentioned punishment, either verbally, literally, as in the case of the one who said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal 8: 32], and the one who said: ﴿Then bring us what you promise us, if you are of the truthful﴾, and other than that of what He related about them. Or by their evil deeds that lead to it and make it obligatory for them figuratively, as is the habit of all of them. And His saying: ﴿and man has ever been hasty﴾ [al-Isra' 17: 11], meaning by "man" those of his individuals to whom the mentioned supplication is attributed. "Hasty" means one who hastens to seek whatever occurs to his mind, heedless of its harm, or one who exaggerates in haste, seeking the punishment while it is certainly coming to him. Thus there is in it a kind of mockery of him. And according to the interpretation that the supplication refers to their deeds, haste is understood as persistence and perseverance in earning the punishment through those deeds.

And according to the second view: the Qur'an calls man to what is better. And he, in some of his times, as in anger, leaves it and supplicates God for himself, his family, and his wealth with what is evil. And man, by his natural disposition, is hasty and impatient, not waiting until what afflicts him passes away. Or he supplicates for what is evil while thinking it good. And man is hasty (p-3909), not discerning, not reflecting on his affairs with due reflection, so as to ascertain what is truly good and worthy of supplication, and what is evil and deserving of seeking refuge from. End.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[12] ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. Then We effaced the sign of the night, and We made the sign of the day to give sight, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. And everything We have explained in detail.﴾

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ That is: We made them, in their forms, their succession, and their variation in length and shortness, as two signs indicating that they have a wise Creator. ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾ That is: by making it dark. ﴿And We made the sign of the day to give sight﴾ That is: bright, for distinguishing perceptible things. The idafa (genitive construction) in both is either explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: the sign which is the night, and the sign which is the day; or it is real (haqiqiyyah). The sign of the night and the day is their two luminaries. The meaning of the effacing of the moon is either its creation with its light obliterated in itself, or the diminishing of what it receives from the sun little by little until the period of its disappearance (al-mahaq). And making the sun give sight means originating it as luminous in itself, possessing rays by which things are seen. Thus the attribution in (giving sight) is metaphorical to the customary cause, or it is a figurative usage through the relation of causation. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿that you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾ are connected to (We made): that you may seek in the day provision from Him, Glorified is He, by dispersing for livelihood, crafts, works, and travels. ﴿And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ That is: the reckoning related to what is contained within the years of months, nights, and days; or the reckoning operating in transactions, such as sales and leases, and in acts of worship; that is, to recognize the passing of the appointed terms set for these matters, for were it not for this, no one would know the computation of times and affairs would be disrupted.

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): This verse is a foundation for the science of timekeeping, astronomy (al-hay'ah), and history. In the verse there is laff and nashr (a figure of speech) that is not in order. End of quote.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And everything﴾ That is: of what you need in your religion and your worldly life. ﴿We have explained in detail﴾ That is: We have made it clear in the Qur'an with an eloquent clarity admitting no ambiguity. Like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of everything﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. Thus its being a guide to that which is most upright became manifestly evident.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 17, verses 13–15:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[13–15] ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird (fate) to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open. "Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant."﴾ ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its detriment. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And We would not punish until We sent a messenger.﴾

﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ means: We have fastened to him his deed that proceeds from him by his own choice, good and bad, such that it never leaves him. Rather, it clings to him like a collar around the neck; it is never separated from him in any way.

Al-Tabari said: The meaning is: And every person We have fastened to him what has been decreed that he will do, and to which he will return, of misery or happiness according to his deed, around his neck, never to leave him. His saying "We have fastened to him his bird around his neck" is an image for what the Arabs used to take as omen or ill omen from the flights and crossings of birds.

That is because the Arabs, when they wanted to undertake one of their affairs, and wanted to know whether that affair would lead them to good or to evil, would consider the state of birds: whether it flies on its own or needs to be startled; and when it flies, whether it flies to the right, or to the left, or upward into the air, and other states which they considered, and by each of which they inferred conditions of good and evil, happiness and misfortune. When this became frequent among them, good and evil were named "the bird," by naming a thing after something that accompanies it.

Al-Tabari said: So He, exalted is His praise, informed them that every person among them has had his Lord fasten to him his bird around his neck, whether that which He fastened of the bird is ill omen and misery leading him to the Fire, or good fortune leading him to the Gardens of Eden. As for why it was attributed to the neck and not to the hand or other limbs of the body, it is said: because the neck is the place of marks, and the place of necklaces and collars and other things that adorn or disgrace. So the speech of the Arabs came to attribute necessary things of the children of Adam and others of that kind to their necks. Their usage of this became so frequent that they attributed all necessary things of the bodies to the necks, just as they attributed the offences of the limbs of the body to the hand, saying: "That is for what his hands have earned," even if it was his tongue or his private part that drew it upon him. Likewise His saying: ﴿We have fastened to him his bird around his neck﴾. Its essence, as al-Razi stated, is that His saying ﴿around his neck﴾ is a metaphor for obligation, as one says: "I placed this around your neck," meaning: I entrusted you with this task and obliged you to keep it. And one says: "I garlanded you with such-and-such and collared you with such-and-such," meaning: I directed it to you and made it binding upon you. From this: "The sultan garlanded him with such-and-such," meaning: the office became, in its binding upon him, in the place of the garland and the position of the collar. From this one says: "So-and-so garlands so-and-so," meaning: he makes that belief like a garland tied around his neck.

His exalted saying ﴿And We will bring out for him﴾ means: We will make manifest for him ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: the raising for the recompense of deeds, ﴿a record which he will find spread open﴾, meaning: he will find it open, containing his good deeds and his bad deeds. And it will be said to him:

﴿Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant﴾ meaning: a witness to what you did.

Al-Qashani said: ﴿a record﴾ is a fashioned form depicting his deeds; ﴿which he will find spread open﴾ because those forms become manifest in him actually, in detail, not folded up as they were when they existed in him potentially. It will be said to him: ﴿Read your record﴾, meaning: read it as one commanded, obeying a commander who orders him to read; or as the angelic faculties command him. Whether he was a reader or not, because the deeds there are represented by their forms and images, which everyone knows, not in the manner of writing with letters, so the unlettered would not know them: ﴿Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant﴾, because his self sees what it did clinging to it, set before its eyes, in detail, so that denial is impossible for it.

As for His exalted saying ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself﴾, Abu al-Su'ud said: it is a summation of what preceded of the Qur'an's guidance to the most upright ways, and of the necessity of deeds for their doers. That is: whoever is guided by its guidance, and acts by what its contents contain of rulings, and refrains from what it forbids, the benefit of his guidance returns only to himself, and does not pass beyond him to another who is not guided. ﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ meaning: from the path to which it guides him, ﴿only goes astray to its detriment﴾ meaning: the burden of his straying falls upon it, not upon anyone else who has not engaged in it. So His saying ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ is a confirmation of what precedes it, for the sake of emphasis on it.

Abu al-Su'ud said: That is, a soul does not carry, as a bearer of burden, the burden of another soul, such that the second soul could be freed from its burden. The necessary connection between the agent and his deed would be disrupted. Rather, each of them bears its own burden. This is the realization of the meaning of His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾. As for what His exalted saying indicates: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes with a bad intercession will have a portion of it﴾ [al-Nisa: 85], and His saying: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and some of the burdens of those whom they misguide without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25], these are about one bearing another's burden, and benefiting from his good deed, and being harmed by his bad deed. In reality this is a benefit from the good deed of his own self and a harm from his own bad deed. For the recompense of the good and bad deeds that the doer performs is necessarily his. What reaches the one who intercedes is the recompense of his intercession, not the recompense of the essence of the good and bad deed. Likewise, the recompense of misguidance is confined to the misguided. What the misleaders bear is the recompense of misleading, not the recompense of going astray.

The emphasis was specifically given to the second clause to cut off vain hopes, since they used to claim that if they were not upon the truth, the responsibility would fall upon their forefathers whom they had followed in imitation. End.

His exalted saying ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ is an explanation of divine care, following the explanation that the effects of guidance and misguidance are specific to their possessors, and that the guided one is not deprived of the fruits of his guidance, and that a soul is not held to account for another's crime. That is: it is not valid, nor fitting from Us, rather it is impossible in Our custom, founded upon profound wisdoms, that We punish a people until We send to them a messenger who guides them to the truth and restrains them from error, to establish the proof and to cut off excuse. And punishment is more general than the worldly and the otherworldly, by His saying: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs before we are humiliated and disgraced?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿Every time a company is thrown into it, its keepers ask them: Did no warner come to you?﴾ ﴿They say: Yes, a warner had come to us, but we denied and said: Allah has revealed nothing; you are only in great error﴾ [al-Mulk: 8–9]. Likewise His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened, and its keepers will say to them: Did there not come to you messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day? They will say: Yes, but the word of punishment has come due upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿They will cry out therein: Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteous deeds other than what we used to do. Did We not give you life long enough that whoever would remember could remember therein, and the warner had come to you? So taste; for the wrongdoers there is no helper﴾ [Fatir: 37]. Among other verses indicating that He, exalted, does not punish a people with a punishment of annihilation, nor cause anyone to enter the Fire except after the sending of messengers.

Qatada said: Indeed Allah, exalted, does not punish anyone until a report or clear evidence has been presented to him, and He does not punish anyone except for his own sin.
