And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And We would not punish until We sent a messenger.﴾

﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ means: We have fastened to him his deed that proceeds from him by his own choice, good and bad, such that it never leaves him. Rather, it clings to him like a collar around the neck; it is never separated from him in any way.

Al-Tabari said: The meaning is: And every person We have fastened to him what has been decreed that he will do, and to which he will return, of misery or happiness according to his deed, around his neck, never to leave him. His saying "We have fastened to him his bird around his neck" is an image for what the Arabs used to take as omen or ill omen from the flights and crossings of birds.

That is because the Arabs, when they wanted to undertake one of their affairs, and wanted to know whether that affair would lead them to good or to evil, would consider the state of birds: whether it flies on its own or needs to be startled; and when it flies, whether it flies to the right, or to the left, or upward into the air, and other states which they considered, and by each of which they inferred conditions of good and evil, happiness and misfortune. When this became frequent among them, good and evil were named "the bird," by naming a thing after something that accompanies it.

Al-Tabari said: So He, exalted is His praise, informed them that every person among them has had his Lord fasten to him his bird around his neck, whether that which He fastened of the bird is ill omen and misery leading him to the Fire, or good fortune leading him to the Gardens of Eden. As for why it was attributed to the neck and not to the hand or other limbs of the body, it is said: because the neck is the place of marks, and the place of necklaces and collars and other things that adorn or disgrace. So the speech of the Arabs came to attribute necessary things of the children of Adam and others of that kind to their necks. Their usage of this became so frequent that they attributed all necessary things of the bodies to the necks, just as they attributed the offences of the limbs of the body to the hand, saying: "That is for what his hands have earned," even if it was his tongue or his private part that drew it upon him. Likewise His saying: ﴿We have fastened to him his bird around his neck﴾. Its essence, as al-Razi stated, is that His saying ﴿around his neck﴾ is a metaphor for obligation, as one says: "I placed this around your neck," meaning: I entrusted you with this task and obliged you to keep it. And one says: "I garlanded you with such-and-such and collared you with such-and-such," meaning: I directed it to you and made it binding upon you. From this: "The sultan garlanded him with such-and-such," meaning: the office became, in its binding upon him, in the place of the garland and the position of the collar. From this one says: "So-and-so garlands so-and-so," meaning: he makes that belief like a garland tied around his neck.

His exalted saying ﴿And We will bring out for him﴾ means: We will make manifest for him ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: the raising for the recompense of deeds, ﴿a record which he will find spread open﴾, meaning: he will find it open, containing his good deeds and his bad deeds. And it will be said to him:

﴿Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant﴾ meaning: a witness to what you did.

Al-Qashani said: ﴿a record﴾ is a fashioned form depicting his deeds; ﴿which he will find spread open﴾ because those forms become manifest in him actually, in detail, not folded up as they were when they existed in him potentially. It will be said to him: ﴿Read your record﴾, meaning: read it as one commanded, obeying a commander who orders him to read; or as the angelic faculties command him. Whether he was a reader or not, because the deeds there are represented by their forms and images, which everyone knows, not in the manner of writing with letters, so the unlettered would not know them: ﴿Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant﴾, because his self sees what it did clinging to it, set before its eyes, in detail, so that denial is impossible for it.

As for His exalted saying ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] himself﴾, Abu al-Su'ud said: it is a summation of what preceded of the Qur'an's guidance to the most upright ways, and of the necessity of deeds for their doers. That is: whoever is guided by its guidance, and acts by what its contents contain of rulings, and refrains from what it forbids, the benefit of his guidance returns only to himself, and does not pass beyond him to another who is not guided. ﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ meaning: from the path to which it guides him, ﴿only goes astray to its detriment﴾ meaning: the burden of his straying falls upon it, not upon anyone else who has not engaged in it. So His saying ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ is a confirmation of what precedes it, for the sake of emphasis on it.

Abu al-Su'ud said: That is, a soul does not carry, as a bearer of burden, the burden of another soul, such that the second soul could be freed from its burden. The necessary connection between the agent and his deed would be disrupted. Rather, each of them bears its own burden. This is the realization of the meaning of His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾. As for what His exalted saying indicates: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes with a bad intercession will have a portion of it﴾ [al-Nisa: 85], and His saying: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and some of the burdens of those whom they misguide without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25], these are about one bearing another's burden, and benefiting from his good deed, and being harmed by his bad deed. In reality this is a benefit from the good deed of his own self and a harm from his own bad deed. For the recompense of the good and bad deeds that the doer performs is necessarily his. What reaches the one who intercedes is the recompense of his intercession, not the recompense of the essence of the good and bad deed. Likewise, the recompense of misguidance is confined to the misguided. What the misleaders bear is the recompense of misleading, not the recompense of going astray.

The emphasis was specifically given to the second clause to cut off vain hopes, since they used to claim that if they were not upon the truth, the responsibility would fall upon their forefathers whom they had followed in imitation. End.

His exalted saying ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ is an explanation of divine care, following the explanation that the effects of guidance and misguidance are specific to their possessors, and that the guided one is not deprived of the fruits of his guidance, and that a soul is not held to account for another's crime. That is: it is not valid, nor fitting from Us, rather it is impossible in Our custom, founded upon profound wisdoms, that We punish a people until We send to them a messenger who guides them to the truth and restrains them from error, to establish the proof and to cut off excuse. And punishment is more general than the worldly and the otherworldly, by His saying: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs before we are humiliated and disgraced?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿Every time a company is thrown into it, its keepers ask them: Did no warner come to you?﴾ ﴿They say: Yes, a warner had come to us, but we denied and said: Allah has revealed nothing; you are only in great error﴾ [al-Mulk: 8–9]. Likewise His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened, and its keepers will say to them: Did there not come to you messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day? They will say: Yes, but the word of punishment has come due upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿They will cry out therein: Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteous deeds other than what we used to do. Did We not give you life long enough that whoever would remember could remember therein, and the warner had come to you? So taste; for the wrongdoers there is no helper﴾ [Fatir: 37]. Among other verses indicating that He, exalted, does not punish a people with a punishment of annihilation, nor cause anyone to enter the Fire except after the sending of messengers.

Qatada said: Indeed Allah, exalted, does not punish anyone until a report or clear evidence has been presented to him, and He does not punish anyone except for his own sin.

And His exalted saying:

The discussion of the words of His saying, the Exalted:

[16] ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they defiantly transgress therein; so the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction.﴾

﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they defiantly transgress therein; so the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction.﴾ This clarifies that the punishment occurs after the message has been delivered, and that it came only because of their rebellion against the messengers and their deviation from their methodology. The verse may indicate that the punishment mentioned earlier is meant as worldly annihilation, since it is confined to that. The meaning: when We intend to punish a people with a punishment of uprooting: ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾, meaning its privileged ones, to obedience through the tongue of the messenger sent to them; ﴿and they defiantly transgress therein﴾ by opposing His command, exalted is He, and departing from His obedience; ﴿so the word becomes due against it﴾, that is, it becomes binding upon it, through their disobedience, their wickedness and their insolence, the threat of God which He had promised to whoever disbelieves in Him and opposes His messengers, namely destruction after the excuse and warning have been given through the messengers and proofs; ﴿and We destroy it with complete destruction﴾, that is, We ruin it with a ruin whose extent cannot be comprehended and cannot be described. We destroy those within it of its people with a terrible destruction, as happened to the House of the Holy Place (Bayt al-Maqdis) when the Jews deviated from their law, as we have previously explained. He specifically mentioned the affluent ones, namely the tyrants, kings and leaders, although the command is directed to all, because they are the foundation of the address and the rest follow them; and because the directing of the command to them is more emphatic. He omitted the object of ﴿We command﴾ because it is evident that what is meant is the truth and the good, especially after mentioning the guidance of the Qur'an to what it guides to. Using "the town" (al-qaryah) rather than its people adds intensification and horror, pointing to the chastisement of them by demolishing their edifices and houses and obliterating their traces, which is more painful to the heart and more wounding to the enemy. For this reason he followed it with the emphatic verbal noun, saying ﴿with complete destruction﴾, that is, total, such that no crop or livestock remained for them.

(p-3915) Al-Qashani said: Everything in this world has a cessation, and its cessation comes through the occurrence of a predisposition that requires it. Just as the cessation of the body comes through the loss of balance and the occurrence of a deviation that removes it from its continuance and stability, so too the destruction and ruin of a city comes through the occurrence of a deviation within it from the straight path, which is the path of God, namely the law that preserves order. When the time comes for the destruction of a town, there must be a deserving of destruction, and that is through wickedness and departure from the obedience of God. When His will became attached to its destruction, there preceded it necessarily first the wickedness of its affluent ones, those of luxury and comfort, through insolence and ingratitude for the blessing of God, and using it for what is not fitting. This was by a command from God and a decree from Him, due to a wretchedness that was entailed by their predispositions. At that point their destruction became obligatory. And the words of His, the Exalted:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[17] ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah? And your Lord is sufficient as one who is Acquainted with and Seeing of the sins of His servants.﴾

﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah?﴾ That is: Many a time have We destroyed the disbelieving nations after the time of Noah, such as 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh, among those whose accounts are related in the Mighty Qur'an and those whose accounts are not related. And "al-qurun" (the generations) is the plural of "qarn," which is applied to a specific period of time, to the people who lived together in it, and to every nation that perished so that none of it remained. He specified "Noah" and did not say "after Adam" because he was the first messenger whose people harmed him, so the punishment completely uprooted them. Therefore, there is in this a threat and a warning to the polytheists.

﴿And your Lord is sufficient as one who is Acquainted with and Seeing of the sins of His servants.﴾ That is: nothing of them is hidden from Him. He perceives their secret and their open, and He will recompense for them.

The verse indicates, as al-Zamakhshari said, that sins are the causes of destruction, because when He followed their destruction with His knowledge of their sins, a more complete knowledge, it indicates that He requited them for them.

(p-3916)

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[18-19] ﴿Whoever desires the immediate, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have made for him Hell, which he will enter, blamed and banished.﴾ ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and exerts the effort due to it while he is a believer - those are the ones whose effort is ever appreciated.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:19]

﴿Whoever desires the immediate, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have made for him Hell, which he will enter, blamed and banished.﴾ ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and exerts the effort due to it while he is a believer - those are the ones whose effort is ever appreciated.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:19]

That is: whoever's aim is the immediate world, and for it he works and strives, and it alone he seeks, not believing in the return, nor hoping for reward or punishment from his Lord despite his knowledge of it: ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend﴾, i.e., what We will of extending the world to him or restricting it for whomever God wishes to do that with. Or of destroying him by what He, exalted is He, wills of His hastened punishments. Then he will burn in Hell in the Hereafter: ﴿blamed﴾ for his scant gratitude to his Master and the evil of his conduct in what preceded: ﴿banished﴾, expelled from mercy, distanced and cast out into the Fire. And whoever desires the Hereafter and seeks it, and works for it the work that is obedience to God and what pleases Him, those - their work is ever appreciated with a good reward.

Note:

Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: This verse falls within the meaning of His words: ﴿And every person We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾ [al-Isra' 17:13]. The first verse refers to one who made the omen of his soul a misfortune, and the second to one who made it a blessing and good. As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and strives for it its striving﴾ [al-Isra' 17:19], i.e., the righteous deeds that are due to it and fitting for it, it clarifies His words: ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter﴾ [al-Isra' 17:19], that desiring it is by striving and toil in contending against falsehood and raising the status of truth, together with being adorned with sound faith, by performing what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden. And His words, Exalted is He:

And His words, Exalted is He:

The discussion of the Exalted's words:

[20–22] ﴿Each We extend, to these and to those, from the bounty of your Lord. And the bounty of your Lord has never been restricted.﴾ ﴿Look how We have favored some of them over others; and the Hereafter is greater in ranks and greater in favoring.﴾ [al-Isra' 21] ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken.﴾ [al-Isra' 22]

﴿Each We extend﴾ means: each one of the two groups. His words ﴿these and those﴾ are a substitute (badal) for "each" (kullan). ﴿From the bounty of your Lord﴾ means: from His grace. He provides for both of them together from His provision until they reach their term and complete their appointed time, what has been decreed for them. Then their conditions diverge after death, and their destinations separate after arrival: the group that desires the immediate life has Hell as its destination, and the group that desires the Hereafter has Paradise as its return. ﴿And the bounty of your Lord has never been restricted﴾ means: it is not withheld, nor is it kept back from a sinner on account of his disobedience. This clause serves as a rationale for the inclusiveness of the extension to both groups.

﴿Look how We have favored some of them over others﴾ [al-Isra' 21] means: in provision in this world. ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in ranks and greater in favoring﴾ [al-Isra' 21] because in it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

Then the Exalted pointed to what attains the ranks of the Hereafter: disavowal of polytheism (shirk), and holding fast to faith (iman) and its branches, through His words: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken.﴾ [al-Isra' 22] meaning: do not make a partner with Him in His worship, lest you become reproached and blamed for polytheism, forsaken by Allah, who will leave you to that partner and will not help you: ﴿And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ [Al 'Imran 160]

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 17, verses 23–24:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[23–24] ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him, and that you be good to parents. Whether one of them or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small."﴾ [al-Isra: 24]

﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ i.e., commanded a matter that is definitively settled: ﴿that you not worship except Him, and that you be good to parents﴾ i.e., and that you be good to your parents with goodness. Al-Qashani said: Glorified and exalted is He has joined the goodness toward parents with monotheism and the singling out of Him in worship, because they are fitting to the presence of Lordship (al-hadrah al-rububiyyah), since they raised you when you were helpless, small, weak, having no power and no movement. They are the first manifestation in which the effects of God's attributes of origination (al-ijad) and lordship, and of mercy and tenderness, appeared toward you. Yet they are in need of having their rights fulfilled, while God is free of need of that. Thus, after monotheism, the most important obligation is honoring them and fulfilling their rights as far as possible: ﴿Whether one of them or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small."﴾ [al-Isra: 24] In this there is an extreme emphasis on honoring parents and being dutiful to them that is not hidden.

﴿Immā﴾ is (in), the conditional particle, to which (mā) has been added for emphasis. ﴿Aḥaduhumā﴾ is the subject (fā'il) of (yablughanna), and ﴿kilāhumā﴾ is conjoined to it. The meaning of {ʿindaka} is that they grow old and become unable, and they become a burden upon their child, with no one else to care for them, so they are with him in his house and under his care. That is harder for him and requires greater endurance and patience. Perhaps he will take on from them what they used to take on from him in childhood. Thus he is commanded to deal with them with gentleness of character, softness of manner and forbearance, so that he does not say to them, when something annoys him that he finds disgusting from them, or something burdens him from their expenses, ﴿uff﴾, let alone anything more than that. So reported al-Zamakhshari.

(p-3919) ﴿And do not repel them﴾ i.e., do not rebuke them with harshness for what does not please you. ﴿But speak to them﴾ instead of the "uff" and the repelling: ﴿a noble word﴾ i.e., a good word, as the goodness of manners toward them requires. The meaning of His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾ [al-Isra: 24] is: humble yourself to them and be modest. In it is a metaphor (istiʿarah) that is both implicit (makniyyah) and imaginative (takhyiliyyah). He likened humility to a bird by an implied comparison, attributed to it a wing by imagination, and lowering by a supporting element (tarshih). ﴿Lowering it﴾ is what a bird does when it gathers its chicks for rearing. Or it is a clear metaphor (istiʿarah tasrihiyyah) in the single word, which is the wing, and the lowering is a supporting element. The ﴿wing﴾ (janah) means the side, as one says "the two wings of the army," and its lowering is a figurative usage, as one says "gentle of side" (layyin al-janib) and "low of side" (munkhafid al-janib). The annexation of the wing to humility is for specification (al-bayan), since it is a descriptive qualifier: that is, your humble wing. In it is emphasis, because it is described by a verbal noun, as if it were made the very essence of humility. Or the construction is a figurative metaphor (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah), and so it is an example for the utmost degree of humility. The secret of mentioning the wing and its lowering is to depict humility as if it were witnessed and perceived by the senses.

And {min} in His saying, ﴿out of mercy﴾ [al-Isra: 24], is causal (ibtida'iyyah) in the sense of causation: i.e., out of the abundance of your mercy toward them and your tenderness toward them, because of their old age and their need today for one who was, yesterday, the neediest of God's creatures toward them. The need of a person for one who was once needy of him is the utmost in humility and lowliness, so he shows him the greatest mercy. As al-Khafaji said:

O you who came asking about my poverty, what is the state of one who asks from one who asks of him?

The humiliation of the sultan is only when he becomes in need of his own subordinate.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small"﴾ [al-Isra: 24] means: O Lord! Show tenderness toward them with Your mercy and forgiveness, as they showed tenderness toward me in my youth, when they had mercy on me and raised me when I was small until I could stand on my own and became independent of them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, do not be content with your mercy toward them, which has no lasting existence, but ask God to have mercy on them with His lasting mercy, and make that a recompense for their mercy toward you in your childhood and their raising you. The kaf is for causation, i.e., for the sake of their raising me.

Al-Tibi said: The kaf is for emphasizing existence, as if it were said: Lord, have mercy upon them with a mercy that is certain, manifest, and without doubt, like His saying: ﴿just as you speak﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 23], and this is a fine interpretation.

(p-3920) Note:

Some of the early scholars recommended that a person supplicate for his parents at the end of the tashahhud just before the salam, because it is a virtuous time. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 17, verses 23–24:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[23–24] ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him, and that you be good to parents. Whether one of them or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small."﴾ [al-Isra: 24]

﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ i.e., commanded a matter that is definitively settled: ﴿that you not worship except Him, and that you be good to parents﴾ i.e., and that you be good to your parents with goodness. Al-Qashani said: Glorified and exalted is He has joined the goodness toward parents with monotheism and the singling out of Him in worship, because they are fitting to the presence of Lordship (al-hadrah al-rububiyyah), since they raised you when you were helpless, small, weak, having no power and no movement. They are the first manifestation in which the effects of God's attributes of origination (al-ijad) and lordship, and of mercy and tenderness, appeared toward you. Yet they are in need of having their rights fulfilled, while God is free of need of that. Thus, after monotheism, the most important obligation is honoring them and fulfilling their rights as far as possible: ﴿Whether one of them or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," and do not repel them, but speak to them a noble word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small."﴾ [al-Isra: 24] In this there is an extreme emphasis on honoring parents and being dutiful to them that is not hidden.

﴿Immā﴾ is (in), the conditional particle, to which (mā) has been added for emphasis. ﴿Aḥaduhumā﴾ is the subject (fā'il) of (yablughanna), and ﴿kilāhumā﴾ is conjoined to it. The meaning of {ʿindaka} is that they grow old and become unable, and they become a burden upon their child, with no one else to care for them, so they are with him in his house and under his care. That is harder for him and requires greater endurance and patience. Perhaps he will take on from them what they used to take on from him in childhood. Thus he is commanded to deal with them with gentleness of character, softness of manner and forbearance, so that he does not say to them, when something annoys him that he finds disgusting from them, or something burdens him from their expenses, ﴿uff﴾, let alone anything more than that. So reported al-Zamakhshari.

(p-3919) ﴿And do not repel them﴾ i.e., do not rebuke them with harshness for what does not please you. ﴿But speak to them﴾ instead of the "uff" and the repelling: ﴿a noble word﴾ i.e., a good word, as the goodness of manners toward them requires. The meaning of His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾ [al-Isra: 24] is: humble yourself to them and be modest. In it is a metaphor (istiʿarah) that is both implicit (makniyyah) and imaginative (takhyiliyyah). He likened humility to a bird by an implied comparison, attributed to it a wing by imagination, and lowering by a supporting element (tarshih). ﴿Lowering it﴾ is what a bird does when it gathers its chicks for rearing. Or it is a clear metaphor (istiʿarah tasrihiyyah) in the single word, which is the wing, and the lowering is a supporting element. The ﴿wing﴾ (janah) means the side, as one says "the two wings of the army," and its lowering is a figurative usage, as one says "gentle of side" (layyin al-janib) and "low of side" (munkhafid al-janib). The annexation of the wing to humility is for specification (al-bayan), since it is a descriptive qualifier: that is, your humble wing. In it is emphasis, because it is described by a verbal noun, as if it were made the very essence of humility. Or the construction is a figurative metaphor (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah), and so it is an example for the utmost degree of humility. The secret of mentioning the wing and its lowering is to depict humility as if it were witnessed and perceived by the senses.

And {min} in His saying, ﴿out of mercy﴾ [al-Isra: 24], is causal (ibtida'iyyah) in the sense of causation: i.e., out of the abundance of your mercy toward them and your tenderness toward them, because of their old age and their need today for one who was, yesterday, the neediest of God's creatures toward them. The need of a person for one who was once needy of him is the utmost in humility and lowliness, so he shows him the greatest mercy. As al-Khafaji said:

O you who came asking about my poverty, what is the state of one who asks from one who asks of him?

The humiliation of the sultan is only when he becomes in need of his own subordinate.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small"﴾ [al-Isra: 24] means: O Lord! Show tenderness toward them with Your mercy and forgiveness, as they showed tenderness toward me in my youth, when they had mercy on me and raised me when I was small until I could stand on my own and became independent of them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, do not be content with your mercy toward them, which has no lasting existence, but ask God to have mercy on them with His lasting mercy, and make that a recompense for their mercy toward you in your childhood and their raising you. The kaf is for causation, i.e., for the sake of their raising me.

Al-Tibi said: The kaf is for emphasizing existence, as if it were said: Lord, have mercy upon them with a mercy that is certain, manifest, and without doubt, like His saying: ﴿just as you speak﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 23], and this is a fine interpretation.

I have gathered from the transmitted supplications for deceased parents, or one of them, a collection that I included in my book "al-Awrad al-Ma'thurah." I still supplicate for them with them in the last part of the night or between the call to dawn prayer and its iqamah, because of the excellence I see in this time over others. And His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[25-27] ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him) repeatedly.﴾ ﴿And give the relative his right, and the needy, and the traveler, and do not spend wastefully.﴾ [Al-Isra: 26] ﴿Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and ever has Satan been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ [Al-Isra: 27].

﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾ i.e., your inner intentions, whether you intend righteousness toward your parents or disobedience: ﴿If you are righteous﴾ i.e., intending uprightness and goodness toward them, without disobedience: ﴿then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him)﴾ i.e., the repentant, those who return to Him, Exalted is He, with regret for what has passed from them, and steadfastness in what has been commanded: ﴿Forgiving﴾ i.e., He forgives them what they have earned. And there is no hiding what the opening of the verse contains of promise to one who harbors goodness, and threat to one who harbors aversion, resentment and disobedience.

It has been said: the verse is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) required by the context of emphasis and stress. As if it were said: how can he fulfill their right when sudden impulses arise? It is answered: when you establish the matter on its foundation, and that is what is constant, and then a momentary lapse occurs without intent to harm, then God's kindness holds back His punishment. It is also permissible, as al-Zamakhshari said, that this be general for everyone who has committed an offense and then repented of it. It includes the one who wronged his parents and repented of his wrong, since it comes after it.

Then, after the injunction concerning the two parents, Exalted is He enjoined concern for relatives other than parents, with His saying, Glorified is He: (p-3921)

﴿And give the relative his right﴾ [Al-Isra: 26] i.e., of his connection, good companionship, and kindness to him by spending on him.

Al-Mahayimi said: He did not say (the near one) because the unqualified term is understood to mean the complete (kinship). Since the attribution (idafa) is for the slightest association, (dhu al-qurba) applies to everyone who has any kinship at all. ﴿And the needy﴾ [Al-Isra: 26] i.e., the poor from among distant relatives. Along with charity to relatives there is the joining of kinship ties. ﴿And the traveler﴾ [Al-Isra: 26] i.e., the wayfarer who has been cut off. That is: help him and strengthen him to complete his journey. It includes what is given to him of mounts, aid, or hospitality, for all of that is part of his right. ﴿And do not spend wastefully﴾ [Al-Isra: 26] i.e., in any manner whatsoever, by spending on what is forbidden or disliked, or on one who does not deserve it, thinking it to be a kindness to yourself or to others. Thus said al-Mahayimi.

In al-Kashshaf: The Jahiliyya used to slaughter their camels and gamble for them, and squander their wealth for boasting and reputation, and they mentioned that in their poetry. So God commanded spending in its proper channels, in what draws one near and brings one closer.

﴿Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils﴾ [Al-Isra: 27] i.e., their likes in ungratefulness for the blessing of wealth by expending it on what is not fitting. This is the utmost blame, for there is no evil worse than Satan's. Or they are their brothers, meaning their followers in companionship and obedience, as a friend obeys his friend and a follower obeys his leader; or they are their companions in the Fire by way of threat. The clause serves as the reason for the prohibition against wastefulness, by explaining that it makes its practitioner joined with them. His saying: ﴿And ever has Satan been ungrateful to his Lord﴾ [Al-Isra: 27] is a completion of the reasoning. Abu al-Su'ud said: i.e., exceeding in ungratefulness for the blessing of God, Exalted is He; because it is his nature to direct all that God, Exalted is He, has given him of powers to other than what they were created for, of kinds of disobedience, corruption on earth, misleading people, moving them to disbelief in God, and ingratitude for His blessings overflowing upon them, and diverting them to other than what God, Exalted is He, has commanded. The singling out of this attribute for mention, from among his other ugly attributes, is to signal that wastefulness, which is an expression for diverting God's blessings to other than their proper use, falls under ungratefulness, which is the opposite of gratitude, which is an expression for directing them to what they were created for. The mention of the attribute of Lordship is to indicate the perfection of his rebelliousness, for ingratitude toward the blessing of the Lord, when Lordship is among the strongest motives to gratitude for it, is the utmost ingratitude and the extreme of misguidance and transgression. End.

The verse has been cited as evidence by those who forbid giving away all of one's wealth in the cause of good, and by those who forbid giving charity with all of one's wealth.

The discussion on the interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:

[28] ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾

﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾ That is: if you turn away from the near of kin, the needy, and the wayfarer, out of shame at refusing them, while waiting for provision from God that you hope will come to you so that you may give it to them, then do not dishearten them. Speak to them a soft, easy word, and promise them a fair promise. Al-Kashshaf says: "(seeking, ibtighaʾ) is placed in the position of its cause, which is the loss (of what is given), and there is subtlety in this. So it is as if that turning away was for the sake of striving on their behalf. This is the placing of the effect in the position of the cause, for the loss is the cause of the seeking."

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: "In this verse is the command to speak a gentle word when there is nothing available to give. Ibn Zayd interpreted it as supplication (du'a), and al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas as a promise (ʿidah)." End of quotation.

It is evident that "the easy word" includes all of this. Al-Mahayimi held that the verse concerns refusing them out of fear that they would spend it on what is not befitting. He said: That is, if your turning away from those whom you wish to benefit is established, seeking mercy from your Lord in withholding from them, lest they fall into extravagance by directing the giving toward wine-drinking or fornication, as you know of their habits, then speak to them in declining a gentle word that is easy for them, as a kindness to them in place of giving. End of quotation.

I have not seen this from anyone else, and the noble wording allows it.

(p. 3923)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 17, verse 29:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[29] ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit reproached and destitute.﴾

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ means: do not withhold your hand from spending and giving to those among those mentioned who have a right, as one whose hand is tied to his neck, unable to take with it or to give. ﴿Nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ means: by squandering and extravagance. Ibn Kathir said: That is, do not be extravagant in spending, so that you give beyond your capacity and expend more than your income. ﴿Lest you sit﴾ means: lest you remain. ﴿Reproached﴾ means: the poor and the relatives reproach you. ﴿Destitute﴾ means: regretful, from (al-hasrah, regret), or cut off from you, with nothing left with you, from (hasarahu al-safar), when the journey has reached him with hardship and worn him down.

In the two prohibitions there are two allegorical metaphors (isti'arat tamthiliyyah). In the first, he likened the conduct of the miser in withholding to one whose hand is chained to his neck, such that he cannot extend it.

In the second, he likened extravagance to the spreading of the palm such that it holds nothing. This is evident. Ibn Kathir took His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then you sit reproached and destitute﴾ to be an example of the ordered rhetorical device of "folding and unfolding" (al-laff wa al-nashr al-murattab). He said: That is, you sit, if you are miserly, reproached, people blaming you and disparaging you, and needing nothing from you, as Zuhayr said in the Mu'allaqah (the celebrated pre-Islamic ode):

Whoever has wealth and is stingy with his wealth toward his people will be done without and disparaged.

And if you extend your hand beyond your capacity, you sit with nothing to spend, and you become like the exhausted (al-hasir), which is the beast that has become unable to continue its journey, so it stops from weakness and incapacity.

(p-3924)

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[30] ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.﴾

﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾ That is: He expands it and constricts it, according to His will and His wisdom. ﴿Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾ That is: Acquainted with their inner states, and Seeing of their outward conditions.

Al-Mahayimi said: Since giving to the near of kin, the needy, and the wayfarer was made obligatory for the preservation of their lives, then preserving the lives of children is more deserving; for this reason the Exalted said:

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[31] "And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is ever a great sin."

"And do not kill your children for fear of poverty; We provide for them and for you" is a prohibition addressed to them against what they used to do in the pre-Islamic age (al-Jahiliyyah) of killing their children, namely their wa'd (burying alive) of their daughters, that is, burying them alive. They used to bury them alive out of fear of want (al-faqah), which is poverty and destitution (al-imlaq and al-faqr), through having to spend on them when they grew up. So God forbade them and guaranteed their provision by His words, "We provide for them," meaning: We alone are the ones who grant their provision, in childhood and in adulthood. His words, "and for you," mean: now, by enriching you. His words, "Indeed, their killing," meaning: for the present poverty and the fear of it in the future, "is ever a great sin," meaning: because it leads to the ruin of the world. And what sin could be greater than that?

(p-3925) Admonition:

His words, "for fear of poverty," indicate that this was what drove them to wa'd, not fear of shame, as they claimed. Al-Mubarrad said in al-Kamil: The Arabs in the pre-Islamic age used to bury their daughters, but this was not practised by all of them. It was only among Tamim ibn Murr, Qays, Asad, Hudhayl, and Bakr ibn Wa'il.

Then he said: What drove them to kill the daughters is indicated by His words, "And do not kill your children for fear of poverty," and His words, "nor shall they kill their children" [al-Mumtahanah: 12]. This is clear report that it was due to need. Some have related that they only did it out of pride (anafah). Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna mentioned that Tamim had refused al-Nu'man the tribute (al-itawah). So he dispatched his brother al-Rayyan ibn al-Mundhir against them, who drove off the camels and took the families captive. Then the Banu Tamim sent a delegation to him. When he saw them, he loved to spare them. So he turned toward the people and they asked him for the women. Al-Nu'man said: Every woman who chooses her father shall be returned to him, and if she chooses her husband, she shall be left with him. So all of them chose their fathers, except the daughter of Qays ibn 'Asim, for she chose her husband 'Amr ibn al-Mushmarij. Thereupon Qays vowed that he would not have a daughter born to him without killing her. This is a pretext used by those who bury, saying: "We did it out of pride," but this has been refuted by what God Almighty revealed in the Qur'an.

Ibn 'Abbas, may God have mercy on him, said (in interpreting this verse): "They did not give inheritance to women, nor did they take as ones to be kept except those who thrust with the spear and defend the sanctuary," meaning the males. "Al-khata' (sin/error) is like al-ithm (sin), in wording and meaning."

When He forbade the killing of children, He then forbade the cutting off of offspring by His words, glorified is He:

The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted:

[32] ﴿And do not approach fornication. Indeed, it is an immorality and an evil way.﴾

﴿And do not approach fornication (al-zina). Indeed, it is an immorality﴾ — i.e., an act that is ugly, extremely so in its ugliness. It necessitates aversion from its perpetrator and the dividing of people (apart) (p-3926). ﴿And an evil way﴾ — i.e., how evil is the path it takes. For it is the seizing of private parts, which leads to disorder in the matter of lineages and the stirring up of strife, seizing (what is not lawful) without any cause, whereas a cause is possible, namely the marriage relationship (sihr) which Allah has legislated. Al-Mahayimi said: ﴿an evil way﴾ because it wastes the desire that was created for the pursuit of offspring, by squandering it. Then He mentioned what is even greater in causing aversion and division, so He, may His majesty be exalted, said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[33] ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing. Indeed, he is supported.﴾

﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾ means: its killing, and it is the soul of a human being. ﴿Except by right﴾ means: except by a cause of right. So it is connected to "do not kill" or it is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating either to the subject of "do not kill" or to its object. It is also permissible for it to be connected to "has forbidden," meaning: He has forbidden its killing except by right. Its right is that it is not to be killed except for apostasy after Islam, or adultery after being married (iḥṣān), or killing in retaliation for a life (qawad).

﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing. Indeed, he is supported.﴾ means: whoever is killed without right, in the manner previously mentioned, We have certainly given to his heir, the one between him and whom there is a kinship that requires the demand for his blood, ﴿authority﴾, meaning: a power over the killer in exacting retribution (qiṣāṣ) from him, or a proof by which he takes action against him. In that case, ﴿let him not commit excess in killing﴾, meaning: he should not kill anyone other than the killer, nor two persons for one killer, as was the custom of the pre-Islamic age (jāhiliyya). When one of them was killed, they would kill a group in return for him. His saying ﴿Indeed, he is supported﴾ is a reason given for the prohibition, and the pronoun refers to the heir. That is: it is sufficient for him that Allah has supported him by making retribution obligatory for him, so let him not seek more than that.

(p-٣٩٢٧)

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[34] ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner until he reaches maturity. And fulfill the covenant; indeed, the covenant is ever [that about which one will be] questioned.﴾

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ means: do not dispose of his property except in the manner that is best, which is to safeguard it for him, to make it grow, and to maintain it. His words, exalted is He, ﴿until he reaches maturity﴾ mark the limit of permissibility of disposing of it in the good manner, meaning: until he reaches the time of his strength in intellect, in managing his property, and in the soundness of his condition in his religion. ﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾ means the contract by which you bind yourselves with people in making peace between the people of war and Islam, and among yourselves as well. And sales, leases, hires and the like. ﴿Indeed, the covenant is ever [that about which one will be] questioned﴾ means: it is something demanded, whereby the one who makes the covenant is required to hold fast to it and not neglect it. Or: its party is questioned about breaking it. The meaning: do not break the lawful covenants between you and those with whom you have made covenants, so that you do not violate them and betray those to whom you gave them.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[35] ﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a true balance. That is better and more favorable in outcome.﴾

﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾ means: complete it when you measure for others, and do not diminish it. ﴿And weigh with a true balance﴾ means: with a sound scale, without crookedness or deception. ﴿That is better﴾ means: for you in your livelihood, because your affairs are well ordered by justice and by giving rights to their owners. ﴿And more favorable in outcome﴾ means: in its consequence and final result, since with it there is no wrong for which one will be held to account on the Day of Resurrection. Then He, exalted is He, commanded the observance of the abstract balance.

(p-3928)

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[36] ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned about.﴾ ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height.﴾ [al-Isra: 37].

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ means: do not follow it in speech or action, attributing it to hearing, sight, or reason. It derives from "qafa atharahu" (he followed his trace), meaning he followed it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The intended meaning is the prohibition against a person saying what he does not know, and acting upon what he does not know. It clearly includes the prohibition against blind imitation (taqlid), because it is following what one does not know to be correct or corrupt. End of quotation.

The many kinds of things that fall under this verse are not hidden: such as the doctrines of the Jahiliyyah concerning the divine and concerning what is forbidden and permitted, false testimony, slander, accusing chaste and unaware women, lying, and what resembles them. ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned about﴾, meaning: its owner will be held accountable for what is attributed to it on the Day of Resurrection. Or the limbs themselves will be questioned, so that they bear witness against their owner.

Al-Mahayimi said: He mentioned hearing first because people most often attribute their statements to it, and he mentioned the heart last because it is the endpoint of the senses. He did not mention the rest, because no statement or action contradicts them.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ [al-Isra: 37], meaning: arrogantly, that is, with the gait of one who is self-admiring and proud, since it grants you neither strength nor elevation. As He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 37], meaning: you will never make a rent in it by your treading upon it and the heaviness of your step. ﴿Nor will you reach the mountains in height﴾ [al-Isra: 37], meaning: you will never rival them by stretching yourself up and extending your stature, as the arrogant person does by affectation. In this there is mockery of the arrogant person, and an indication that such conduct is a boast against the earth and against some of its parts.

(p-3929) Al-Nasir said: In this mockery and rebuke there is sufficiency for restraining those who habitually adopt this gait. God has preserved the common people of our time from this gait, while our reciters and jurists have fallen into it. One of them, as soon as he has learned two issues or has two students seated before him, or has grasped a thread of worldly leadership, begins to strut in his walk, swaying and not thinking that he is stretching toward the mountains; rather, he rubs the crown of his head against the clouds of the sky, as though they pass by him while he turns away from them. What benefit is it to him that he recites the Qur'an or that it is recited to him, when his heart is far removed from reflecting upon it? And God is the Giver of success.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1-2] ﴿All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord.﴾ ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom. And do not make with Allah another deity lest you be thrown into Hell, blamed and banished.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:39].

﴿All that﴾ means: what has been forbidden, from His saying: ﴿And do not make with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Isra' 17:39], up to this point: ﴿its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord.﴾ Al-Mahayimi said: As for shirk (association of partners with Allah), it is because it violates the absolute perfection which cannot be conceived alongside shirk. As for worshipping other than Him, it is because it involves glorifying, in the manner specific to Him, one who possesses absolute perfection, so it is in the meaning of shirk. As for disobedience to parents (uquq), it is because it is ingratitude for the blessing of the two parents in raising, which a person needs most. Withholding rights out of miserliness is neglect, and extravagance and overspending are excess. Both are blameworthy, and what is blameworthy is hateful. Killing prevents wisdom from reaching its perfection... Fornication and the squandering of an orphan's property are of the same meaning. Breaking a covenant disrupts the order of the world. Likewise, following what one has no knowledge of. Arrogance is among the attributes of the Real (al-Haqq). And it is the custom of kings to dislike that anyone should take anything from their specific possessions.

﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾ [al-Isra' 17:39], i.e., of that which the intellect judges to be sound and by whose example the soul is reformed.

Al-Mahayimi said: i.e., of the firm knowledge that does not change through doubt: ﴿And do not make with Allah another deity (p-3930) [al-Isra' 17:39]. He repeated it to draw attention to the fact that tawhid is the beginning and end of the matter, and that it is the head of every wisdom and its foundation. Whoever lacks it, his knowledge and judgment will not benefit him.

Abu al-Su'ud said: He has ordered upon it what is the outcome of associating partners, first, when it is said: ﴿So you will sit blamed and forsaken﴾ [al-Isra' 17:22], and He has ordered upon it here a result in the Hereafter, so it is said: ﴿then you will be thrown into Hell, blamed﴾ [al-Isra' 17:39], i.e., with great ignominy, ﴿banished﴾ [al-Isra' 17:39], i.e., removed and expelled from mercy. And in the mention of the casting, in the passive form, there is a conformity to the ways of majesty, and a contempt for the polytheist, and making him like a piece of wood that someone takes in his hand and throws into the furnace. End of quotation. And His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[40] ﴿Has your Lord then favored you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels? Indeed, you utter a grave saying.﴾

﴿Has your Lord then favored you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels? Indeed, you utter a grave saying.﴾

This is an address to those among the idolaters of the Arabs who said, "The angels are the daughters of God." The interrogative hamza is for denial and rebuke.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: Has your Lord singled you out, in purity and exclusivity, with the best of children, who are the males, and not given them a share for Himself, while He has taken for Himself the lesser of them, who are the daughters, which you yourselves do not accept for your own selves, but bury alive and kill? This is contrary to wisdom and to what your reason and customs dictate. For slaves are not given the finest and purest of things, while the worst and lowest of them is assigned to the masters.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, you utter a grave saying﴾, means: by attributing children to Him, which is a characteristic of created things, and then by preferring yourselves over Him, since you assign to Him what you dislike.

(p-3931)

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 17, verses 41–42:**

**The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:**

[41–42] ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an that they may be reminded, but it increases them in nothing but aversion.﴾ ﴿Say, "If there were with Him other gods, as they say, then they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne."﴾ [al-Isra': 42].

﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an﴾: that is, We repeated the clarification for the people in many aspects, and We made clear in it every kind of example. ﴿that they may be reminded﴾: that is, that they may take heed and be at ease with what is used as proof against them. ﴿but it increases them﴾: that is, the diversification mentioned. ﴿in nothing but aversion﴾: that is, aversion from the truth and distance from it, which the aspects of clarification would bring them close to.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If there were with Him other gods, as they say, then they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne."﴾ [al-Isra': 42]. That is: Say to these polytheists (who claim that God has partners from among His creation, worshipping others besides Him, so that those partners might bring them near to Him in nearness), "If the matter were as you say, and there were with Him gods worshipped to bring one near to Him and to intercede with Him, then those worshipped beings would worship Him and draw near to Him, and seek nearness and obedience with Him. So worship Him alone, as those whom you call upon besides Him worship Him. You have no need of a worshipped being to be an intermediary between you and Him, for He does not love that and does not approve of it, but rather He dislikes it and rejects it. He has forbidden it through the tongues of all His messengers and prophets." This is what Ibn Kathir chose, and Ibn Jarir preceded him to it.

Its essence: the "way" (sabil) means the means that leads to Him. Within this there is an indication of a categorical syllogism (qiyas iqtirani), which is formulated as follows: "If it were as you claim, that there were with Him gods, they would have drawn near to Him. And everyone who is like this is not a god. Therefore, they are not gods."

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿then they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Isra': 42] is: they would have sought a way to Him by contention and opposition, as is the custom of kings with one another, following the manner of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been within them gods other than God, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. This view was preferred by al-Zamakhshari over the first. Abu al-Su'ud said: it is the more apparent and more fitting, in light of His words:

(p-3932)

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on the verses 43–44 of Surah al-Isra':

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[43–44] ﴿Glory be to Him, and He is exalted far above what they say, high and great.﴾ ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ [al-Isra': 44].

﴿Subhanahu﴾: it is clear that the intent is to explain that what they say necessarily entails a grave matter that they do not reckon. As for seeking a means of access to Him, exalted is He, through drawing near (to Him), this is not something specific to this statement, nor is it something that entails for them what they do not perceive; rather, it is a matter they hold to outright. End of quote. The meaning of ﴿Subhanahu﴾ is: He is transcendent above having offspring or partners, a transcendence that befits Him. ﴿Wa-ta'ala 'amma yaquluna 'uluwwan kabira﴾ means: He has magnified Himself greatly above that. Indeed, such calumny and slander are things from which His exalted station is far removed.

Al-Shihab said: He mentioned exaltedness after His description as ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, which is at the highest level of eloquence. As for His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ [al-Isra': 44], it means: God is transcendent, and the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them of creatures sanctify Him and exalt Him above what the polytheists ascribe to Him. All of them bear witness to His oneness in His divinity and lordship, as He said: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth splits open and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90] ﴿that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son﴾ [Maryam: 91]. And His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44], means: because they are different from your languages.

Ibn Kathir said: This is general over animals, inanimate objects and plants, according to the more well-known of the two opinions. Then he cited what is authentically reported of the glorification of food and of pebbles, which came in the Sahihayn and the Masanid and is well known. (p-3933) Al-Raghib chose this in his (Mufradat) and said: It is glorification in the literal sense, by the indication of His saying: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44], and by the indication of His saying: ﴿and whoever is in them﴾ [al-Isra': 44] after mentioning the heavens and the earth. It is not valid that its implied meaning be (whoever is in the heavens glorifies Him and whoever is in the earth prostrates to Him), because we do understand that, and because it is impossible that this be its implied meaning. Then He conjoins to it with His saying ﴿and whoever is in them﴾ [al-Isra': 44], and all things glorify Him and prostrate to Him, some by compulsion and some by choice. The verse indicates that the things mentioned glorify by choice, because of the indication mentioned. End of quote.

Many scholars held that the glorification mentioned is figurative, in the manner of the metaphorical or consequential metaphor, like the expression "the state spoke," for glorification is borrowed to indicate the existence of a capable, wise, necessarily existent Agent, transcendent above offspring and partners, just as an effect indicates its cause. That indicative sign is thus treated as if it were a declaration of His transcendence above what contradicts Him.

"And in everything there is a sign indicating that He is the One."

They said: The address in His saying ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44] is to the polytheists, meaning: because of your failure to apply the correct reflection by which their glorification is understood. Imam Ibn Hazm exaggerated in refuting the first view and choosing the second in his book "al-Milal wa al-Nihal," and there is no harm in citing it, for its strangeness.

He, may God have mercy on him, said in refuting one who said, "Indeed among beasts are messengers": God, exalted is He, only addresses with proof those who understand it. God, exalted is He, said: {O people of understanding}, and we know by necessary reason that God, exalted is He, specifically endowed with speech—which is the disposal of sciences and the knowledge of things as they are, and the disposal of crafts in their variety—humankind alone. We add to them, by true report, the jinn and the angels. Then he, may God have mercy on him, said: Foolishness has led some to attribute discernment to inanimate objects, based on such as His saying ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44] and similar verses. There is no proof for them in it; (p-3934) because the Qur'an must be taken in its apparent sense, and likewise the speech of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Whoever opposes that is disobeying God, Mighty and Majestic, altering His words, unless there is a text on one of the two, or a certain consensus, or a sensory necessity contrary to its apparent sense, in which case one stops there. Whoever takes it in its apparent sense then is ascribing falsehood to God, Mighty and Majestic, or lying about Him and His Prophet, peace be upon him—we seek refuge in God from both.

Since we have previously shown by necessary proofs that animals (other than humans, jinn and angels) have no speech—meaning they have no disposal of sciences and crafts—and this statement is witnessed by the senses and known by necessity, denied only by a shameless one obstinate against his own senses; and we have shown that whatever is contrary to the discernment familiar to us is not discernment; and this too is known by necessity, direct observation and witnessing; it is therefore necessary that it is contrary to what is called in the Law and the language speech, utterance, glorification and prostration. So it is necessary that these are homonymous terms whose wordings coincide, while their meanings differ, and it is not permissible for anyone to take them to other than this; for if he does, he would be reporting that God, exalted is He, said what observation and the intellect by which we know God, exalted is He, refute—and without which we would not know Him.

So the wording is shared, and the meaning is what the evidence establishes. The explanation: glorification for us is nothing but the saying "Glory be to God and praise Him"; and we know by necessity that stones, wood, insects, vermin and colours do not say "Subhan Allah" with its letters—this no one with a grain of sound intellect doubts. Since there is no doubt in this, we know with certainty that the glorification God mentioned is true and is a meaning other than our glorification, beyond doubt. Since there is no doubt in this, glorification in the origin of the language is the exalting of God, exalted is He, above evil. Since this is established, every thing in the world is, without doubt, exalting God, exalted is He, above the evil which is the attribute of having come into being. There is nothing in the world but that it indicates—by what is in it of signs of craftsmanship and by its requiring a Maker who resembles nothing—that God, exalted is He, is transcendent above every (p-3935) evil and deficiency; and this is what many people do not understand or comprehend, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44]. This is the glorification of everything with the praise of God, exalted is He, beyond doubt. And this meaning is true, which no monotheist denies. If our statement is agreed upon as sound, and necessity requires that it is not the glorification familiar to us, then our statement is established and the statement of whoever opposed us by his supposition is negated.

Also, God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44]. The atheist materialist is a thing, of which no one doubts that it is a thing, and he never glorifies God, exalted is He, with praise; so it is established by necessity that the unbeliever glorifies, since he is among the things that glorify God, exalted is He. And his glorification is certainly not his saying "Glory be to God and praise Him." Rather, it is the exalting of God, exalted is He, through the proofs of His creation and composition, above the Creator resembling anything He has created. This is certain, beyond doubt.

It is thus established by what we have mentioned that the word "tasbih" (glorification) is among the homonymous terms, which apply to two kinds or more. End of his words.

Its summary: denial that inanimate objects have glorification and discernment in the sense found in humans. This is true, with no doubt, and it is not permissible for anyone to deny it. However, it does not negate that they have a glorification and a discernment suited to them, so the disagreement returns to being verbal. Modern science, as some scholars have said, now agrees that there is in matter a trace of life, and that it possesses all the essential attributes that distinguish living things; that what is in the individual atoms and the fine particles of matter is not dead, but are living, moving elements having a form of the lower life observed in all kinds of matter, such as attraction, repulsion, being affected by external influences, changes in the balance of forces, particles gathering into regular shapes according to limited structures, and secreting various chemical compounds. In sum, what the new science says about the resemblance of non-living bodies to living bodies corresponds to the conceptions of the ancients and the poets in this matter. End of quote.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾ [al-Isra': 44], meaning: in that He did not hasten to punish them despite their disbelief and their deficiency in reflection. Had they repented, He would have forgiven them what had proceeded from them.

(p-3936) Then God, exalted is He, depicted the state of the polytheists with the noble Revelation, when the Messenger, God's blessings be upon him, recites it to them, calling them to act upon what it contains of monotheism and rejecting polytheism and their other errors, likening them to one whose insight, sight and hearing have been sealed, in His saying, exalted is He:

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on the verses 43–44 of Surah al-Isra':

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[43–44] ﴿Glory be to Him, and He is exalted far above what they say, high and great.﴾ ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ [al-Isra': 44].

﴿Subhanahu﴾: it is clear that the intent is to explain that what they say necessarily entails a grave matter that they do not reckon. As for seeking a means of access to Him, exalted is He, through drawing near (to Him), this is not something specific to this statement, nor is it something that entails for them what they do not perceive; rather, it is a matter they hold to outright. End of quote. The meaning of ﴿Subhanahu﴾ is: He is transcendent above having offspring or partners, a transcendence that befits Him. ﴿Wa-ta'ala 'amma yaquluna 'uluwwan kabira﴾ means: He has magnified Himself greatly above that. Indeed, such calumny and slander are things from which His exalted station is far removed.

Al-Shihab said: He mentioned exaltedness after His description as ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, which is at the highest level of eloquence. As for His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ [al-Isra': 44], it means: God is transcendent, and the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them of creatures sanctify Him and exalt Him above what the polytheists ascribe to Him. All of them bear witness to His oneness in His divinity and lordship, as He said: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth splits open and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90] ﴿that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son﴾ [Maryam: 91]. And His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44], means: because they are different from your languages.

Ibn Kathir said: This is general over animals, inanimate objects and plants, according to the more well-known of the two opinions. Then he cited what is authentically reported of the glorification of food and of pebbles, which came in the Sahihayn and the Masanid and is well known. (p-3933) Al-Raghib chose this in his (Mufradat) and said: It is glorification in the literal sense, by the indication of His saying: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44], and by the indication of His saying: ﴿and whoever is in them﴾ [al-Isra': 44] after mentioning the heavens and the earth. It is not valid that its implied meaning be (whoever is in the heavens glorifies Him and whoever is in the earth prostrates to Him), because we do understand that, and because it is impossible that this be its implied meaning. Then He conjoins to it with His saying ﴿and whoever is in them﴾ [al-Isra': 44], and all things glorify Him and prostrate to Him, some by compulsion and some by choice. The verse indicates that the things mentioned glorify by choice, because of the indication mentioned. End of quote.

Many scholars held that the glorification mentioned is figurative, in the manner of the metaphorical or consequential metaphor, like the expression "the state spoke," for glorification is borrowed to indicate the existence of a capable, wise, necessarily existent Agent, transcendent above offspring and partners, just as an effect indicates its cause. That indicative sign is thus treated as if it were a declaration of His transcendence above what contradicts Him.

"And in everything there is a sign indicating that He is the One."

They said: The address in His saying ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44] is to the polytheists, meaning: because of your failure to apply the correct reflection by which their glorification is understood. Imam Ibn Hazm exaggerated in refuting the first view and choosing the second in his book "al-Milal wa al-Nihal," and there is no harm in citing it, for its strangeness.

He, may God have mercy on him, said in refuting one who said, "Indeed among beasts are messengers": God, exalted is He, only addresses with proof those who understand it. God, exalted is He, said: {O people of understanding}, and we know by necessary reason that God, exalted is He, specifically endowed with speech—which is the disposal of sciences and the knowledge of things as they are, and the disposal of crafts in their variety—humankind alone. We add to them, by true report, the jinn and the angels. Then he, may God have mercy on him, said: Foolishness has led some to attribute discernment to inanimate objects, based on such as His saying ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies [Him] with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44] and similar verses. There is no proof for them in it; (p-3934) because the Qur'an must be taken in its apparent sense, and likewise the speech of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Whoever opposes that is disobeying God, Mighty and Majestic, altering His words, unless there is a text on one of the two, or a certain consensus, or a sensory necessity contrary to its apparent sense, in which case one stops there. Whoever takes it in its apparent sense then is ascribing falsehood to God, Mighty and Majestic, or lying about Him and His Prophet, peace be upon him—we seek refuge in God from both.

Since we have previously shown by necessary proofs that animals (other than humans, jinn and angels) have no speech—meaning they have no disposal of sciences and crafts—and this statement is witnessed by the senses and known by necessity, denied only by a shameless one obstinate against his own senses; and we have shown that whatever is contrary to the discernment familiar to us is not discernment; and this too is known by necessity, direct observation and witnessing; it is therefore necessary that it is contrary to what is called in the Law and the language speech, utterance, glorification and prostration. So it is necessary that these are homonymous terms whose wordings coincide, while their meanings differ, and it is not permissible for anyone to take them to other than this; for if he does, he would be reporting that God, exalted is He, said what observation and the intellect by which we know God, exalted is He, refute—and without which we would not know Him.

So the wording is shared, and the meaning is what the evidence establishes. The explanation: glorification for us is nothing but the saying "Glory be to God and praise Him"; and we know by necessity that stones, wood, insects, vermin and colours do not say "Subhan Allah" with its letters—this no one with a grain of sound intellect doubts.
