They have believed in it and affirmed it, and it was established for them that he is the Arab Prophet promised in their Books. When it is recited to them, they fall down in prostration and glorify God, magnifying His command and His fulfilment of what He promised in the revealed Books, and what He gave good news of concerning the sending of Muhammad, peace and blessings of God be upon him, and the sending down of the Qur'an upon him. This is what is meant by the promise in His saying: "the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled" [17:108].

If you ask: What is the explanation of "Indeed, those who were given knowledge"? Is it a reason for what? I say: It may be a reason for His saying "Believe in it or do not believe," and it may be a reason for "Say" by way of consolation to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him, and to comfort his heart. As if it were said: Be consoled regarding the faith of the ignorant by the faith of the scholars. And according to the first: "If you do not believe in it, [then] indeed there has believed in it one who is better than you."

If you ask: What is the meaning of falling down upon the chin? I say: It is falling upon the face. The chin was mentioned, which is the meeting-place of the two jaws, because the one prostrating first meets the earth with the chin of his face. If you ask: The preposition of elevation (ʿalā) is apparent in meaning, when you say "he fell upon his face and upon his chin," so what is the meaning of the preposition lām in "fell for his chin and for his face"? He said: [the poet's line] "So he fell prostrate for the two hands and for the mouth." I say: Its meaning is that he made his chin and his face ready for falling, and he specified it with this because the lām indicates specification.

If you ask: Why did he repeat "fall down upon the chins"? I say: Because of the difference of the two states: their falling while in the state of prostrating, and their falling while in the state of weeping. End of quotation.

Admonition:

The description of these people and their praise for falling down weeping indicates the recommendation of weeping and humble submission. For every praiseworthy quality and attribute by which God the Exalted describes those among His servants whom He loves, it is necessary to adopt it; and whatever blameworthy quality He condemns in them, which He detests, must be avoided.

Al-Imam al-Ghazali, in *al-Ihya'*, counted weeping among the outward etiquettes of recitation. He said: Weeping is recommended along with the recitation. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him, said: "Recite the Qur'an and weep; and if you do not weep, then feign weeping." Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: When you recite the prostration of Subhan (17), do not hasten to prostrate until you weep; and if the eye of one of you does not weep, then let his heart weep. The way to force weeping is to bring sorrow to the heart, for from sorrow weeping arises. The way to bring sorrow is to reflect upon what it contains of threat, warning, covenants and pledges; then to reflect upon one's shortcoming in His commands and prohibitions, so he will inevitably grieve and weep. If sorrow and weeping do not come to him, as they come to the people of pure hearts, then let him weep over the loss of sorrow and weeping, for that is the greatest of calamities. End of quotation.

al-Suyuti mentioned in *al-Iklil* that al-Shafi'i used as evidence His saying, exalted is He: "and they say, 'Exalted is our Lord'" [17:108], etc., for the recommendation of this remembrance in the prostration of recitation.

And His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[110-111] ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names. And do not be loud in your prayer or silent therein, but seek between that a way.﴾ ﴿And say: All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has not had a partner in dominion, and has not had any protector out of weakness; and magnify Him with [full] magnification.﴾ [al-Isra: 111]

﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾: a rejection of what the polytheists denied concerning the naming of the Most Merciful, and a permission to name Him by it. That is: name Him by this name or by that. The "or" (aw) is for choice. ﴿Whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾: that is, whichever of these two names you name and mention, it is good. The statement ﴿to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ has been placed in its position for emphasis and to indicate what the evidence points to, since the excellence of all His names requires the excellence of those two names. The evidence of the answer has thus been put in its place, and that is more eloquent.

The meaning of their being the most beautiful names is that they are independently endowed with the meanings of praise, sanctification and exaltation. This verse is like His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer﴾: that is, in the recitation of your prayer, by an omitted modifier, or by calling the recitation "prayer" because it is one of its most important pillars, just as a unit of prayer is called a rak'ah. ﴿Or silent therein﴾: that is, conceal and hide it. ﴿But seek between that a way﴾: that is, between loudness and silence, a moderate course. For the best of matters is their moderate middle.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The expression "way" (sabil) for that is because it is a matter toward which those who turn (to Allah) direct themselves, which those who follow aim at, and which conveys them to the goal.

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to raise his voice in his recitation. When the polytheists heard it, they would make noise and revile, so He commanded him to moderate his voice so that the polytheists would not hear, and so that those behind him would hear his recitation.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear His worthiness of praise, by His specialness in the attributes of perfection and the qualities of majesty, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say: All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son﴾ [al-Isra: 111]: that is, He has not been a cause for anything existing of his kind, because the effect must necessarily be dependent upon Him, contingent in essence, and non-existent in reality. How then could it be of the kind of the existent in truth, He who is necessary in His essence in every respect? ﴿And has not had a partner in dominion﴾ [al-Isra: 111]: that is, one who equals Him in the power of dominion and sovereignty, from a partner in possession. Otherwise they would be two sharing in necessity of existence and reality. The distinction of each of them from the other must then be by something other than the necessary reality, so their composition would follow, and both would be contingent rather than necessary. Also, if neither can independently act, neither would be a god. If one alone is independent, then that one is the god and not the other, so there is no partner for Him. If both are independent, it follows that two independent agents would converge upon one effect, if they act together; otherwise it follows that the divinity of one to the exclusion of the other, whether he is pleased with its action or not. This was conveyed by al-Qashani.

﴿And has not had any protector out of weakness﴾ [al-Isra: 111]: that is, a helper from weakness and one who prevents it from Him, because of His might. Or: He has not befriended anyone out of some humiliation in order to repel it through his friendship. ﴿And magnify Him with [full] magnification﴾ [al-Isra: 111]: that is, exalt Him above anything of these deficiencies reaching Him, with a sublime magnification.

Completed is what we have annotated on this noble surah, in the forenoon of Saturday, 26 Shawwal, in the year 1323, at the portico of the Sinaniyya Mosque in Damascus, al-Sham. May Allah facilitate for us its completion by His help, and praise is due to Allah alone.
